The Gray Death Infiltrator Suit is a medium battle armor design manufactured by Defiance Industries on Furillo. Introduced in 3102 as a successor to the aging Infiltrator Mk. I, the suit fills the scout and skirmisher role with a highly mobile platform built for precision aerial insertion and modular mission flexibility. Nicknamed the Quokka, it can be configured with five distinct equipment packages for roles ranging from direct combat to sensor deployment and target designation.

The Firedrake configuration mounts a Firedrake Support Needler with thirty rounds of ammunition in the modular weapon mount, complementing the suit's fixed David Light Gauss Rifle. The needler excels at suppressing and eliminating conventional infantry, making this the preferred loadout for operations where unarmored troops are the primary threat. Basic Manipulators on each arm and Basic Stealth armor are standard across all Infiltrator configurations.

A Parafoil allows precision aerial insertion, and the suit's 90-meter jump range provides solid tactical mobility. Ground speed reaches 32 km/h. The combination of Light Gauss Rifle for ranged anti-armor work and needler for close-in anti-infantry makes the Firedrake configuration well balanced for general-purpose operations.

The Gray Death Infiltrator Suit entered service in 3102 as a Defiance Industries product manufactured on Furillo. Designed as a successor to the aging Infiltrator Mk. I, the new suit filled the scout and skirmisher role that the LCAF had long struggled to address with available battle armor designs. Nicknamed the Quokka, the suit incorporated a Parafoil system for precision aerial insertion, giving drop commanders a level of accuracy previously unavailable with standard battle armor deployment methods.

Defiance built the Infiltrator around a modular weapon mount philosophy, offering five distinct equipment packages that allowed the suit to fill roles from anti-infantry work to sensor deployment and target designation. This flexibility made the Quokka attractive to LCAF commanders who needed a single platform that could be reconfigured for different mission profiles without maintaining separate suit types in their logistics chain. Production at Furillo continued through the Dark Age and into the ilClan era.

The Mines configuration equips the Infiltrator with a Mine Dispenser carrying two mines, adding area denial capability to the suit's reconnaissance portfolio. The David Light Gauss Rifle provides direct-fire capability, and all standard systems including Basic Stealth armor, Parafoil, and 90-meter jump range are retained.

Troopers can deploy mines along enemy approach routes, at chokepoints, or around objectives before withdrawing under stealth. The limited supply of two mines requires careful placement for maximum effect. This configuration sees use in defensive preparations and ambush operations where disrupting enemy movement is more valuable than sustained combat engagement. The combination of stealth insertion via Parafoil and mine deployment makes the configuration effective for covert area denial.

The Remote Sensor configuration carries a Remote Sensor Dispenser with six sensors, allowing troopers to seed an area with autonomous detection devices and withdraw to a safe distance. The David Light Gauss Rifle remains for self-defense. Basic Stealth armor, Parafoil, and standard mobility are unchanged from other configurations.

This loadout extends the Infiltrator's intelligence-gathering reach beyond line of sight. Deployed sensors continue monitoring an area after the trooper has moved on, feeding data back through the suit's communications systems. The configuration is especially useful for establishing sensor networks along approach routes or around high-value installations. Once the dispenser is empty, the trooper effectively reverts to a lightly armed scout.

The Sensors configuration mounts an Improved Sensors package in the modular weapon mount, enhancing the Infiltrator's already capable detection systems. Combined with the Basic Stealth armor and Parafoil insertion capability, this loadout optimizes the suit for deep reconnaissance missions. The David Light Gauss Rifle provides the trooper's only weapon system.

The doubled sensor capability makes this configuration the premier scouting variant of the Infiltrator family. Troopers can detect hidden units, map enemy positions, and relay intelligence at ranges beyond what other configurations can achieve. Ground speed of 32 km/h and 90-meter jump range allow rapid repositioning between observation points. The limitation is obvious: without a secondary weapon, troopers caught in close combat have few options beyond withdrawal.

The TAG configuration replaces the Firedrake needler with a Light TAG system, transforming the Infiltrator into a forward observer platform. The David Light Gauss Rifle remains for self-defense and opportunistic engagements, while the TAG designates targets for friendly artillery and semi-guided munitions. Basic Stealth armor, Parafoil, and 90-meter jump range carry forward.

This loadout pairs well with combined-arms formations that include artillery or units carrying semi-guided missiles. The Infiltrator's stealth characteristics make it an effective TAG platform, as troopers can approach designation range with reduced risk of detection. The trade-off is the loss of anti-infantry firepower, leaving the trooper dependent on the Light Gauss Rifle as a sole weapon system.

The Gray Death Scout Suit is a light battle armor design created by Gray Death Legion technicians on Glengarry. Developed alongside the Gray Death Standard from NAIS-supplied Inner Sphere Standard prototypes, the Scout took a radical approach by sacrificing weapons and heavy armor in favor of enhanced sensors, communications, and mobility. First fielded in 3052, the suit earned a reputation as one of the most capable reconnaissance platforms available to Inner Sphere forces, filling a niche that heavier combat-oriented battle armor could not address.

The Reaper configuration adds offensive capability to the Scout Suit's reconnaissance platform. A Clan-manufactured Machine Gun and Clan Flamer replace the emphasis on pure scouting, giving troopers meaningful firepower against conventional infantry, unarmored vehicles, and exposed equipment. The Improved Stealth armor and Improved Sensors carry forward from the base configuration, preserving the suit's low sensor signature and battlefield awareness.

Armored Gloves and the Jump Booster are retained, maintaining the exceptional mobility and anti-BattleMech capability that define the Scout platform. The use of Clan weaponry reflects the growing availability of Clan-tech components through mercantile channels. The trade-off is straightforward: the Reaper gives up the Light Active Probe for weapons that let scout teams handle threats they would otherwise need to avoid or call in support against.

When the New Avalon Institute of Science distributed prototypes of its Inner Sphere Standard battle armor to elite units in 3050, the Gray Death Legion proved an inspired choice of recipient. The mercenary command had long emphasized infantry operations, particularly anti-BattleMech tactics, and their experienced technicians brought a practical perspective that pure laboratory researchers lacked. By late 3051, Legion engineers had split the NAIS prototype into two distinct derivatives. While one became the Gray Death Standard, the other took a far more radical direction.

The Scout Suit stripped away more than half the prototype's armor and all integrated weaponry. In their place, Legion technicians installed enhanced sensor arrays, long-range communications gear, and an improved jump pack. The mechanical claws gave way to fully articulated armored gloves that preserved a trooper's natural dexterity for handling infantry weapons and placing satchel charges. The result was a suit built for deep reconnaissance rather than direct combat, a concept without equivalent among existing battle armor designs.

The Scout made its combat debut on Pandora in 3052, fighting alongside the Gray Death Standard against Clan Jade Falcon forces near the town of Vandmaal. In thick jungle terrain, Scout-equipped troopers leveraged their advanced sensors and enhanced mobility to locate and outmaneuver Clan positions. Springing from concealment, the Legion's armored infantry destroyed two OmniMechs and crippled three more with well-placed satchel charges.

Following the Truce of Tukayyid, the Gray Death Legion continued limited production on Glengarry. Most suits replaced the Legion's own combat losses, though small numbers were sold to other mercenary commands and the Lyran Alliance Armed Forces. The Legion's destruction on Hesperus II in 3065 during the FedCom Civil War ended this arrangement. Surviving support staff established Gray Death Technologies on Glengarry with backing from Defiance Industries, continuing Scout Suit production for the LAAF and mercenary buyers.

The Word of Blake's assault on Glengarry in 3074 destroyed the GDT factory. Defiance Industries absorbed the remnants of the company and relocated all Gray Death battle armor production to Furillo. The Scout Suit's original design was preserved through this transition and remains in production. Its influence extended beyond the Gray Death line: the Jump Booster system pioneered on the Scout was later adopted by Clan Nova Cat engineers for the Clan Battle Armor design, and the emphasis on stealth and sensor capability shaped an entire generation of light battle armor across the Inner Sphere.

The Gray Death Scout Suit carries no integral weapons, relying on the trooper's ability to wield conventional small arms through its Armored Gloves. This design choice freed mass for a Light Active Probe and long-range communication systems that give the suit exceptional battlefield awareness. A Jump Booster pushes the suit's maximum jump range to 120 meters, far exceeding most battle armor designs of its era. Improved Stealth armor provides solid protection while dramatically reducing the suit's sensor signature.

At 750 kilograms, the Scout is among the lightest operational battle armor designs. The gloves preserve enough manual dexterity for satchel charge placement and handling of infantry weapons, making even an unarmed Scout trooper dangerous to careless BattleMech pilots. The lack of integral weapons is the suit's most significant limitation, leaving troopers dependent on carried arms for any engagement beyond anti-BattleMech attacks.

The Gray Death Standard Suit is a medium battle armor design created by Gray Death Legion technicians alongside the Scout Suit. Derived from NAIS-supplied Inner Sphere Standard prototypes, the Standard retained the original design's combat focus while incorporating improvements suggested by the Legion's experienced infantry troops. Fielded in 3052, the suit offered a flexible combination of solid protection, modular firepower through interchangeable weapon mounts, and proven reliability that made it a mainstay of Lyran battle armor formations for decades after the Legion's dissolution.

The Flamer configuration mounts a standard Flamer in the Gray Death Standard's modular weapon mount, optimized for anti-infantry work and area denial. The left arm retains its Battle Claw for anti-BattleMech attacks and OmniMech transport, while an Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount on the same arm handles light targets. Improved Sensors mimic the function of portable radar, detecting hidden opponents and enhancing the trooper's situational awareness.

Standard armor provides 450 kilograms of protection, enough to absorb significant weapons fire while keeping the trooper operational. Ground speed reaches 32.4 km/h over open terrain, adequate for keeping pace with advancing infantry formations. The Flamer's limited range and ammunition independence make it best suited for close-quarters engagements and urban fighting where suppressing infantry in confined spaces is more valuable than ranged precision.

The Gray Death Standard emerged alongside the Scout Suit in late 3051, the second of two derivatives created by Gray Death Legion technicians from NAIS-supplied Inner Sphere Standard prototypes. Where the Scout stripped the prototype down for reconnaissance, the Standard took a more conservative approach: enhancing the original design's capabilities while retaining its fundamental role as a medium battle armor platform. Legion engineers responded to their troops' assessments by adding an anti-personnel weapon, improved sensors, and a more capable sensor suite while keeping the modular weapon mount that gave troopers flexibility in the field.

The Standard made its combat debut alongside the Scout on Pandora in 3052 against Clan Jade Falcon forces. Near Vandmaal, Gray Death Standard troopers proved decisive in the jungle fighting, reinforcing conventional infantry against BattleMech opposition. The suit's thick armor gave troopers the confidence to close with Clan OmniMechs, and the combination of battle claw and modular weaponry made each trooper a genuine threat. Word of the mercenaries' success spread quickly through AFFC channels.

Production on Glengarry remained limited, focused on the Legion's own needs with occasional sales to other mercenary units and the LAAF. The Gray Death Legion was destroyed on Hesperus II in 3065, one of many casualties of the FedCom Civil War. Surviving personnel founded Gray Death Technologies with Defiance Industries' financial support, establishing a dedicated factory on Glengarry. As the only battle armor manufacturer within the Lyran Alliance, GDT found a ready market for the Standard among LAAF commands and mercenaries alike.

In 3068, Word of Blake forces raided the Glengarry factory, looting equipment and slaughtering the Brewer's Legion security force. GDT managed to restart limited production by 3073, but Precentor Berith's second attack in 3074 was thorough enough to render the facility inoperable. Defiance Industries completed its buyout of Gray Death Technologies and moved production to Furillo, where it resumed by the early 3080s. The Standard's modular weapon mount accepted a Light Recoilless Rifle starting in 3069, expanding the suit's engagement options without requiring structural changes to the chassis.

The Standard has remained in continuous production longer than any other Gray Death design. Its combination of solid protection, modular firepower, and proven reliability ensured demand even as newer and more specialized battle armor entered the market. Across the Lyran Commonwealth and among mercenary commands throughout the Inner Sphere, the Gray Death Standard remains a common sight on battlefields where powered infantry are called to fight.

The Laser configuration equips the Standard Suit with a Small Laser, providing reliable direct-fire capability without ammunition dependency. The Battle Claw, Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount, and Improved Sensors all carry forward from the base platform. This loadout offers the best sustained firepower of the Standard's weapon options, as the energy weapon can fire indefinitely without resupply concerns.

The Small Laser's effective range and damage output make it useful against both infantry and light armored targets. Against BattleMechs, the laser supplements the Battle Claw's swarming attacks with focused energy damage to exposed components. The 450 kilograms of standard armor and 32.4 km/h top speed remain consistent across all Standard configurations, giving commanders predictable performance regardless of weapon selection.

The Light Recoilless Rifle configuration became available in 3069, expanding the Standard Suit's modular weapon options. The LRR provides effective anti-armor capability at longer range than the SRM launcher, with a ballistic profile that experienced infantry troopers find intuitive. The weapon bridges the gap between the Small Laser's sustained fire and the SRM's heavy warhead.

The Battle Claw, Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount, Improved Sensors, and 450 kilograms of standard armor carry forward. The LRR's ammunition supply requires management, but its versatility against both armored and soft targets makes this configuration popular among units that face mixed opposition. The later introduction date means fewer LRR-equipped Standards are in service compared to the original four weapon options.

The Machine Gun configuration emphasizes anti-infantry volume of fire. The weapon's high rate of fire makes it devastating against conventional troops and effective at suppressing soft targets in prepared positions. The Battle Claw, Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount, and Improved Sensors are retained, as are the 450 kilograms of standard armor and 32.4 km/h ground speed.

Ammunition dependency is the Machine Gun's primary limitation, requiring troopers to manage their expenditure across an engagement. The weapon is less effective against hardened targets than the Small Laser or SRM options, making this configuration best suited for operations where the primary threat is conventional infantry rather than armored opponents.

The SRM configuration mounts a single-tube SRM Launcher with a four-missile magazine, giving the Standard Suit its heaviest anti-armor punch. The missile's warhead can threaten light vehicles and damage BattleMech components at ranges beyond the Battle Claw's reach. The Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount, Improved Sensors, and 450 kilograms of standard armor remain standard across the platform.

Limited ammunition is the configuration's defining constraint. Four missiles must be carefully allocated across an engagement, and resupply in the field is impractical for battle armor. Once expended, the trooper falls back on the Battle Claw and anti-personnel weapon for offensive capability. Commanders typically reserve SRM-equipped troopers for specific hardened targets rather than general infantry support.

The Gray Death Strike Suit is a medium battle armor design developed by Gray Death Technologies in the early 3070s. Created to give the Lyran Commonwealth a dedicated fire support battle armor platform, the Strike combined missile armament with target designation capability in a well-armored package that could soften enemy positions before heavier forces closed the distance. The production model entered service in 3080 after a protracted development process that began with a Clan-technology prototype.

The HarJel variant incorporates self-sealing technology that automatically patches breaches in the suit's armor, maintaining atmospheric integrity in hostile environments. Advanced armor replaces the standard plating, providing equivalent protection at reduced weight and freeing mass for the HarJel system and a Firedrake Needler for anti-infantry work. The SRM-3 launcher and Light TAG system carry forward from the production model.

Basic Manipulators and ground-only movement remain consistent with the base Strike platform. The HarJel system broadens the suit's operational envelope to include vacuum, underwater, and contaminated atmosphere operations where a single armor breach could prove fatal. This makes the variant particularly valuable for boarding actions and operations on worlds with hazardous conditions.

The Gray Death Strike Suit was born from desperation. In the early days of the Jihad, Word of Blake forces sacked the Gray Death Technologies factory on Glengarry in 3068, causing widespread damage and killing the Brewer's Legion defenders. The attack did not completely shut down production, and GDT devoted its remaining resources to developing more potent battle armor to fight the Word of Blake. The result was a hybrid design combining Inner Sphere and Clan technology, built under the supervision of technician Brian Kinnison.

The prototype removed the Standard Suit's improved sensors and modular weapon mount. In their place, Kinnison's team mounted a Clan-specification Advanced SRM-3 launcher and a Light TAG system for designating targets for artillery and guided munitions. Both arms retained Battle Claws, and the anti-personnel weapon mount was preserved. The reliance on Clan components proved to be the prototype's greatest weakness. Defiance Industries attempted to secure a steady supply of the advanced launchers from the Diamond Sharks and other Inner Sphere-friendly Clans, but none were willing to provide enough to justify mass production.

Precentor Berith's second assault on Glengarry in 3074 destroyed the GDT factory entirely. Defiance Industries absorbed the company and relocated manufacturing to Furillo, but production of any Gray Death battle armor stalled for years during the transition. When the Strike Suit finally entered production in late 3080, Defiance had redesigned it around Inner Sphere components. The Clan advanced launcher gave way to an Inner Sphere equivalent with two reloads, and the Battle Claws were replaced with lighter Basic Manipulators to accommodate the heavier weapon system. The Light TAG system was retained, giving troopers who jettisoned their spent missile pack continued usefulness as forward observers.

Sale of the production Strike Suit was restricted to the Lyran Commonwealth, helping the LCAF rebuild its battle armor strength after Jihad losses. The suits saw action primarily in raids against remnants of the Free Worlds League. Defiance Industries also maintained a small stock for its own security forces, rumored to be the original Clan-tech prototypes rather than the production model. The HarJel variant, introduced in 3107, incorporated self-sealing technology and upgraded to advanced armor, broadening the suit's operational envelope for hostile environment operations.
BA Harjel not coded. Unit included for completeness

The prototype Strike Suit mounts a Clan-specification Advanced SRM-3 launcher with three shots, delivering greater effective range and hitting power than the production model's Inner Sphere equivalent. A Light TAG system in the left arm provides target designation capability, and both arms end in Battle Claws rather than the production model's Basic Manipulators. The Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount is retained.

Mixed Clan and Inner Sphere technology classifies the prototype as experimental. The 450 kilograms of standard armor and ground-only movement profile match the production model, but the Clan launcher must be jettisoned before anti-BattleMech attacks can be performed. The dependence on Clan-sourced components limited the prototype's operational availability and complicated logistics for any unit fielding the suit alongside Inner Sphere standard equipment.

The production Gray Death Strike Suit mounts a detachable SRM-3 launcher with two reloads as its primary armament, paired with a Light TAG system for designating targets for friendly artillery and semi-guided munitions. Basic Manipulators replace the prototype's Battle Claws, and an Anti-Personnel Weapon Mount handles infantry-scale threats. The launcher can be jettisoned after expenditure, slightly improving the suit's ground speed and allowing the trooper to continue contributing as a forward observer through the TAG system.

At 1,000 kilograms with 450 kilograms of standard armor, the Strike Suit is a well-protected medium platform. It lacks jump capability entirely, relying on a powerful ground movement system that reaches 32 km/h over open terrain. The absence of jump jets limits the suit's tactical flexibility in rough terrain but simplifies maintenance and reduces the training burden on new troopers. The Strike operates best in a fire support role, softening targets with missiles before heavier forces close the distance.

shared: The Grenadier is an assault-weight Inner Sphere battlesuit developed by the Hahm-Heinze Design Bureau for the Armed Forces of the Federated Suns. Designed to mount the heaviest weapon systems possible on a single suit frame, the Grenadier prioritized raw firepower over mobility or protection. The suit carries a fixed missile launcher, a modular weapon mount accommodating a range of battlefield roles, and an anti-personnel station for close-range defense. Standard stealth armor provides electronic signature reduction, though total protection is modest for the weight class. At two thousand kilograms, the Grenadier is too heavy for OmniMech transport, restricting deployment to ground-based insertion methods.

This configuration integrates a battle armor C3 computer system with a heavy recoilless rifle and Firedrake support needler. The C3 network link allows troopers to share targeting data with other networked units, improving accuracy across the entire formation. The heavy recoilless rifle delivers greater kinetic energy than the standard light version, effective against medium armor at moderate range. The Firedrake needler handles anti-personnel duties at close quarters. As a networked fire support platform, the configuration's value scales with the size and coordination of the C3 network it operates within. In isolation, the suit loses the network's accuracy bonuses and functions as a competent but unremarkable ballistic combatant. The absence of a missile system reduces anti-armor punch compared to other Hunter-Killer variants.

The Hahm-Heinze Design Bureau began developing what would become the Grenadier when NAIS first started producing battle armor for the Federated Commonwealth. Drawing on long-standing ties to General Motors' plants on Talcott and Salem, the firm had access to early prototypes that informed their work. Nearly a decade of development produced a concept focused on mounting the heaviest possible weapon systems on a single suit. Hahm-Heinze approached the AFFC in 3062 with the finished design and two prototypes, but the FedCom Civil War consumed resources and attention, and the Federated Commonwealth initially passed on the Grenadier.

Only after the conflict demonstrated the suit's battlefield potential did production begin in earnest, with General Motors on Talcott and Albion Advanced Technologies on New Avalon manufacturing the design. Sales remained steady but slow through the Jihad years, hampered by disrupted supply lines and transportation. GM responded with an aggressive public relations effort called "Operation Parade," recruiting retired armored infantrymen to demonstrate the suit's effectiveness in field exercises and actual combat deployments alongside AFFS commands. The campaign proved successful enough that GM began offering alternative weapon configurations based on accumulated field reports and combat data.

Pairing a Magshot gauss rifle with a small variable speed pulse laser, this Hunter-Killer configuration delivers accurate, sustained firepower across a range of engagement distances. The variable speed pulse laser adjusts its pulse rate to optimize accuracy against targets at different speeds, making it effective against fast-moving vehicles and infantry alike. The Magshot provides precise kinetic strikes at medium range, while the Firedrake support needler covers close-range anti-personnel work. The combination of energy and ballistic weapons reduces ammunition dependency compared to purely projectile-based loadouts, giving troopers better endurance in extended operations. The configuration lacks missile armament entirely, trading the explosive punch of other Hunter-Killer variants for consistent accuracy and sustained damage output across multiple engagement types.

The Grenadier is an assault-weight battlesuit massing two thousand kilograms, built around a fixed short-range missile launcher with seven reloads that gives it exceptional staying power in sustained engagements. The standard configuration mounts a small laser in the left arm modular weapon slot, providing reliable energy firepower that complements the missile system at close range. An anti-personnel weapon mount on the right arm handles unarmored threats. Standard stealth armor makes the suit harder to target, though its total protection is equivalent to the lighter Inner Sphere Standard suit, a modest amount for an assault-class design. Ground speed of twenty-one kilometers per hour is respectable for the weight class, but the lack of jump capability limits the suit's ability to exploit vertical terrain or rapidly reposition during engagements.

The Grenadier II is a heavy-class battlesuit produced by General Motors as an evolution of the original Grenadier design. Incorporating Clan-specification armor technology on an Inner Sphere chassis, the suit achieves comparable protection to its predecessor at a reduced weight of fifteen hundred kilograms. This lighter mass enables OmniMech transport, a capability the heavier Grenadier lacks. The suit features dual modular weapon mounts accommodating a wide variety of loadout configurations and a basic manipulator for environmental interaction. Mixed Inner Sphere and Clan technology gives the Grenadier II a competitive edge in firepower and protection, though the hybrid construction carries a maintenance burden that field technicians have found challenging to manage.

The Grenadier II is a heavy-class battlesuit massing fifteen hundred kilograms, built on an Inner Sphere chassis fitted with Clan-specification standard stealth armor. This mixed-technology approach delivers protection and signature reduction comparable to the assault-weight Grenadier at significantly reduced weight, enabling OmniMech transport that the original cannot support. Configuration A mounts a small laser in the left arm modular weapon slot and a Clan-specification short-range missile launcher with eight reloads in the body mount. A basic manipulator on the right arm allows interaction with objects and terrain. This general-purpose combat loadout benefits from improved ground speed over the heavier Grenadier. The Clan-sourced components carry a maintenance burden, and field technicians accustomed to purely Inner Sphere equipment have found the hybrid systems difficult to service.

General Motors developed the Grenadier II at their Talcott facility as a lighter evolution of the original Grenadier already fielded by the AFFS. The suit entered service in 3137, taking advantage of Clan-specification components made available through Republic of the Sphere trade channels. The AFFS had long proven resistant to fielding heavy battle armor, preferring either the raw power of assault-weight suits or the greater mobility of medium designs. The Grenadier II's reduced mass and mixed-technology construction addressed both concerns, earning acceptance where the heavier original had faced reluctance.

The Republic Armed Forces also acquired the design through Republic-friendly agencies in the Federated Suns. The First Davion Guards were among the earliest units to field the Mk. II, pairing them with Ziblers from the Eighteenth Shibata Recon Regiment as quick reaction forces against Senate rebels. The RAF reserved one configuration exclusively for Republic use, equipping it with indirect fire systems for self-supporting artillery capability. The Republic later exploited this configuration for covert raids beyond the Fortress walls, using what appeared to be Davion equipment to divert suspicion from Republic involvement in border operations.

Configuration B replaces the left arm weapon with a battle armor C3 computer system, transforming the Grenadier II into a networked coordination platform. The body-mounted Clan-specification long-range missile launcher with eight reloads provides indirect fire capability at extended range. The C3 link shares targeting data across networked formations, improving accuracy for all connected units. This configuration trades direct-fire lethality for force multiplication, making it most effective within a larger C3 network alongside more heavily armed suits or vehicles. The long-range missiles allow troopers to contribute firepower from covered positions, reducing exposure. Without the network link active, the configuration offers only modest standalone combat capability, relying entirely on the missile launcher for offensive output.

Configuration C mounts a flamer on the left arm and a medium laser in the body weapon slot, creating a close-to-medium range energy weapon platform. The medium laser provides significantly more firepower than the small lasers found on other configurations, giving troopers genuine anti-armor capability at moderate range. The flamer handles anti-infantry and area denial duties at close quarters. Neither weapon requires ammunition, giving the configuration effectively unlimited endurance in sustained engagements. This energy-focused loadout pairs well with aggressive tactical employment where resupply is uncertain. The configuration's weakness lies in its lack of missile armament, reducing burst damage potential against heavily armored targets, and the flamer demands dangerous closing distance to employ effectively.

Exclusive to Republic of the Sphere forces, Configuration D pairs a Firedrake support needler on the left arm mount with a tube artillery system and eight-round magazine in the body. The tube artillery gives individual troopers organic indirect fire capability, a rare asset at the battle armor scale. Troopers can deliver area bombardment without relying on external fire support assets, making the configuration self-sufficient in suppression and area denial roles. The Firedrake needler provides close-range anti-personnel defense. This configuration's experimental technology classification reflects its cutting-edge systems, and the maintenance challenges shared by all Grenadier II variants are compounded by the artillery system's complexity. The tube artillery's limited magazine and minimum range restrict its usefulness in close-quarters engagements.

The CEX-205 Groundhog is a combat engineering exoskeleton produced by Blue Shot Weapons on Solaris VII. Introduced in 3062, the Groundhog was designed as a field-ready engineering platform capable of supporting military and mercenary operations through a modular manipulator system that allows rapid reconfiguration for different tasks. The suit's interchangeable tool mounts accept a wide range of equipment, from armored gloves suitable for light combat duties to specialized industrial tools for heavy labor, mine clearance, and salvage work. An integrated searchlight and onboard mission equipment storage further extend the Groundhog's operational utility. Heavily armored for an exoskeleton, the Groundhog earned a reputation as one of the first truly battlefield-ready engineering exoskeletons available on the open market.

The Armored Glove configuration equips the CEX-205 with reinforced gauntlets on both manipulator mounts, giving operators the ability to handle standard infantry weapons and conduct anti-BattleMech swarm and leg attacks. At four hundred kilograms, the Groundhog is a maximum-weight exoskeleton protected by one hundred kilograms of standard armor, enough to resist small arms fire but offering little protection against heavier ordnance. The suit's ground speed of thirty kilometers per hour keeps pace with foot infantry, though the lack of jump capability limits vertical mobility in urban or broken terrain.

An integral searchlight supports low-visibility operations, while the body-mounted mission equipment storage bay provides one hundred forty-five kilograms of carrying capacity. Of the Groundhog's available configurations, the Armored Glove loadout is the most combat-oriented, though operators should not mistake the suit's ability to engage BattleMechs for genuine offensive power. The Groundhog remains an engineering platform pressed into a combat-adjacent role, not a dedicated fighting suit.

Blue Shot Weapons had long served a niche market on Solaris VII, producing industrial exo-suits primarily sold to arena management companies for routine maintenance and emergency MechWarrior extractions. The CEX-205 Groundhog, introduced in 3062, marked a deliberate shift in the company's ambitions. Drawing on advances in Inner Sphere battle armor technology, Blue Shot designed the Groundhog as their first truly field-ready combat engineering exoskeleton, offering military and mercenary units a rugged, modular platform far beyond their earlier commercial-grade offerings.

Blue Shot marketed the full line of manipulator configurations in paired sets, emphasizing the suit's adaptability for diverse field operations. Arena operators on Solaris VII also adopted the Groundhog for "tunnel rat" operations during the FedCom Civil War, using the suit's improved communications equipment and searchlight for underground engagements.

The Word of Blake invasion of Solaris VII in 3068 dealt a severe blow to Blue Shot Weapons. The company's production facilities suffered catastrophic damage during the fighting, with capacity reportedly falling below ten percent. By 3071, the damage proved insurmountable, and the Groundhog was officially discontinued. Persistent rumors of a jump-capable variant designated the CEX-250 Leapfrog had circulated for some time, but with the Blue Shot plant in ruins, the design never reached production.

The Basic Manipulator configuration mounts standard dexterous manipulators on both arms, providing operators with the fine motor control needed for general-purpose field work. Like all Groundhog configurations, the suit weighs four hundred kilograms and carries one hundred kilograms of standard armor, sufficient against small arms fire but inadequate against battlefield weapons. Ground speed reaches thirty kilometers per hour with no jump capability.

The Basic Manipulator loadout retains the ability to conduct swarm and leg attacks against BattleMechs and can employ standard infantry weapons, making it functionally similar to the Armored Glove configuration in combat situations. Where the two diverge is in utility: the Basic Manipulator's articulated fingers excel at tasks requiring precision handling, from field repairs to equipment setup. The integrated searchlight and mission equipment bay round out the configuration's support capabilities. The lack of specialized tooling makes this the most general-purpose of the Groundhog's standard configurations, trading task-specific efficiency for broad adaptability.

The Cargo Lifter configuration replaces the Groundhog's standard manipulators with heavy-duty lifting mechanisms rated for one ton of cargo per suit. This makes the configuration invaluable for forward supply operations, ammunition handling, and rapid battlefield logistics work that would otherwise require heavier equipment. The suit retains the standard four-hundred-kilogram frame with one hundred kilograms of standard armor and a ground speed of thirty kilometers per hour. No jump capability is available.

The body-mounted mission equipment bay adds another one hundred forty-five kilograms of internal storage capacity beyond the external lifting capability, and an integral searchlight supports operations in low-visibility conditions. The trade-off for the Cargo Lifter's hauling ability is the complete loss of combat capability. The lifting mechanisms cannot conduct anti-BattleMech attacks or handle infantry weapons, leaving operators entirely dependent on accompanying security elements. In contested zones, Cargo Lifter-equipped Groundhogs must operate under escort, a limitation that restricts their tactical flexibility compared to the combat-capable configurations.

The Industrial Drill configuration mounts paired drilling assemblies on the Groundhog's modular adaptors, providing operators with the tools needed for excavation, fortification construction, and demolition work. The drills can bore through reinforced materials at speeds far exceeding manual methods, making this configuration particularly valuable for combat engineering tasks such as preparing defensive positions, cutting through obstacles, and creating improvised access points.

The standard four-hundred-kilogram chassis carries one hundred kilograms of armor and moves at thirty kilometers per hour without jump capability. The integrated searchlight and mission equipment bay support extended field operations. While the drilling assemblies are not designed as weapons, they pose an obvious threat in close quarters. The Industrial Drill configuration cannot conduct standard anti-BattleMech attacks or employ infantry weapons, however, limiting the operator's options if threatened directly. Groundhogs equipped with this loadout typically work alongside combat-configured suits that can provide security during engineering operations.

The Mine Clearance configuration equips the Groundhog with specialized detection and disposal gear designed for clearing minefields and unexploded ordnance. The modular adaptors mount mine clearance equipment on both arms, allowing operators to locate, identify, and neutralize explosive devices while protected by the suit's one hundred kilograms of standard armor. At four hundred kilograms and thirty kilometers per hour ground speed, the Groundhog provides mine clearance teams with protection well beyond what conventional disposal equipment offers, though the armor remains insufficient against anything heavier than small arms fire.

The suit lacks jump capability, requiring operators to traverse mined areas on foot. The searchlight aids in visual identification of surface-laid devices, while the mission equipment storage bay can carry additional detection instruments or disposal charges. Mine clearance is inherently slow and deliberate work, and the Groundhog's modest speed is rarely a limitation. The configuration sacrifices all combat capability, leaving operators unable to conduct anti-BattleMech attacks or carry infantry weapons.

The Salvage Arm configuration mounts paired salvage manipulators on the Groundhog's modular adaptors, providing light but dexterous grasping tools designed for battlefield recovery and repair work. The salvage arms feature clamp-style manipulators and integrated cutting tools well suited to stripping components, handling ammunition, and conducting field repairs on damaged equipment. At four hundred kilograms with one hundred kilograms of standard armor, the Groundhog offers salvage crews meaningful protection in post-battle environments where unexploded ordnance and unstable wreckage present constant hazards.

Ground speed of thirty kilometers per hour allows operators to reach salvage objectives in reasonable time, though the lack of jump capability limits access to elevated or obstructed wreckage sites. The integral searchlight proves especially valuable during nighttime recovery operations, and the mission equipment bay provides internal storage for recovered components or tools. As with most non-combat configurations, the Salvage Arm loadout cannot conduct anti-BattleMech attacks or employ infantry weapons, requiring escort in unsecured areas.

The AIX-210 Hantu is an armored infantry exoskeleton derived from the CEX-205 Groundhog. Produced by the Kandersteg Foundry Alpha on the Lyran Commonwealth world of Kandersteg, the Hantu was introduced in 3124 as a purpose-built enhancement for conventional infantry formations. The Kandersteg Militia licensed the Groundhog's base design from Blue Shot Weapons and adapted it with stealth armor sourced from Clan Wolf-in-Exile, creating a low-profile exoskeleton intended to improve the survivability of regular foot soldiers rather than replace dedicated battle armor troopers. Formally designated the "Ghost" for its stealth characteristics, most operators instead call the suit the "Jenglot" in wry acknowledgment of how the exoskeleton measures against true battlefield threats.

The AIX-210 mounts armored gloves on both hands and basic myomer augmentation that allows operators to carry conventional infantry weapons and equipment with reduced fatigue. Stealth armor provides a lower sensor signature than standard armor plating, improving the suit's survivability against detection-dependent weapons systems. The suit lacks jump jets, integrated weapons, and specialized equipment such as HarJel, keeping the design simple and the training requirements low. Ground speed and overall handling mirror the Groundhog's performance profile.

The Hantu's primary limitation is that it remains an exoskeleton, not true battle armor. Protection is sufficient against small arms and fragmentation but inadequate against anti-armor weapons or direct BattleMech engagement. The design deliberately avoids the complexity that would require battle armor-level training, trading combat power for accessibility and rapid fielding. Two hundred kilograms of unused capacity in the baseline model allows field customization, though the standard AIX-210 configuration leaves this weight unallocated.

The Kandersteg Militia developed the AIX-210 after officers observed the Groundhog's modular flexibility and recognized an opportunity to address a long-standing vulnerability in their conventional infantry battalions. Even the lightest powered armor offered dramatically better protection than standard infantry kit, and the Militia sought to close that gap without the expense and training overhead of fielding true battle armor. Blue Shot Weapons, whose Solaris VII production lines had been destroyed decades earlier, licensed the Groundhog's base design to Kandersteg, providing the engineering foundation for what became the Hantu.

Kandersteg's engineers stripped away the Groundhog's modular adaptor system and focused on protection and simplicity. Stealth armor manufactured for Clan Wolf-in-Exile was integrated into the design, giving the suit a low sensor signature that its operators could exploit in defensive and ambush situations. The Hantu deliberately retained the Groundhog's ergonomic, transparent control interface, which had been designed for minimally trained civilian users. This decision proved critical to the Militia's training doctrine, which emphasized treating Hantu-equipped soldiers as enhanced conventional infantry rather than battle armor troopers.

Two hundred kilograms of unused capacity in the baseline model spawned a family of AIX-21x sub-variants incorporating sensors, electronic warfare packages, and integrated weapons. The Kandersteg Militia purchased these sparingly, but mercenary commands passing through Kandersteg's hiring halls spread the design well beyond its intended user base.

The Hauberk is an Inner Sphere assault battle armor developed by the Armed Forces of the Federated Suns during the Jihad. Built by General Motors on Salem, the two-thousand-kilogram suit was derived from Clan Goliath Scorpion's Undine chassis, repurposed from its original aquatic role into a ground-based heavy infantry platform. The Hauberk's thick armor and powerful armament made it one of the most heavily equipped battle armor designs fielded by the Federated Suns, filling a defensive assault role that had previously been dominated by Clan designs.

The base Hauberk configuration mounts one of the most potent weapon systems found on battle armor: a five-tube long-range missile rack with five salvos of ammunition, positioned behind the head on the suit's torso. This gives a squad the combined firepower to threaten BattleMechs and vehicles from well beyond typical infantry engagement ranges. A small laser in a fixed right-arm mount provides secondary firepower at shorter distances, while a battle claw allows the trooper to engage in close combat despite the suit's inability to perform anti-BattleMech swarming attacks.

The Hauberk's improved stealth armor is its defining defensive feature, allowing squads to set up ambushes and engage targets before they can effectively return fire. At two thousand kilograms, the suit is too large to ride OmniMechs into battle and moves at only ten kilometers per hour on the ground, limiting it to defensive operations or requiring armored personnel carrier transport. The lack of anti-personnel weapons leaves the suit exposed to conventional infantry at close quarters, though the battle claw partially offsets this gap.

The Hauberk traces its origins to the Federated Suns' acquisition of Clan Goliath Scorpion's Undine battle armor through Clan Diamond Shark during the Jihad. The AFFS had hoped to field the Clan suits directly, but the Undine's aquatic specialization and chronic maintenance difficulties rendered it impractical for general combat use. Researchers at the New Avalon Institute of Science recognized that the Undine chassis offered a more refined foundation than anything the Inner Sphere had produced, and used it to develop a new assault suit to challenge established designs like the Kanazuchi and Golem.

With Word of Blake forces devastating manufacturing centers on New Avalon, the AFFS contracted General Motors on Salem to handle production. Armed with data recovered from the NAIS before its destruction, GM delivered prototypes by 3069 and achieved full-scale production by 3070. The suit quickly found favor with front-line formations including the Crucis Lancers, Avalon Hussars, and March Militia, though deployment remained constrained by production capacity. Combat experience during the Jihad exposed the base design's close-range limitations, driving the development of specialized configurations. Tech Sergeant Timothy Balke assembled hybrid suits from salvage on New Avalon, and Albion Advanced Technologies later formalized these urban combat lessons into the Commando configuration, which entered production in 3088.

The Commando configuration replaces the Hauberk's standard armament with an urban-fighting loadout built around detachable weapon mounts. Each arm carries a standard extended-range small laser, while a Magshot Gauss Rifle sits over the right shoulder. A twin-tube short-range missile launcher provides a single salvo for close encounters. Mimetic armor allows the Commando to blend into its surroundings, fading from sight between engagements.

Designed for reliability and ease of supply, the Commando uses exclusively Inner Sphere manufactured weapons. The trade-off is reduced long-range capability compared to the base Hauberk, but the mix of energy and ballistic weapons gives troopers consistent firepower in the tight confines of urban terrain. Ground speed remains ten kilometers per hour, though the suit can double that by ejecting its detachable weapon packs. Without battle claws, the Commando cannot ride BattleMechs or OmniVehicles, requiring troop transports to reach operational areas. Once in position, the suit excels at ambush tactics, striking from concealment before disappearing again.

The U15 hybrid configuration packs an eclectic mix of Clan-manufactured weapons onto a modified Hauberk frame using three detachable weapon mounts. A Clan ER small laser occupies the left arm mount, a Clan micro pulse laser sits in the right arm, and a Clan SRM-2 with four reloads is carried on the body alongside a shoulder-mounted Magshot Gauss Rifle. A Clan ECM suite disrupts enemy targeting systems, complementing the suit's mimetic armor salvaged from destroyed Purifier adaptive suits.

This experimental configuration carries more weapon diversity than any standard Hauberk variant, giving troopers options across multiple engagement ranges. The reliance on Clan-manufactured components presents significant logistical challenges, as replacement parts require either salvage or trade with Clan merchants. Movement remains unchanged at ten kilometers per hour with no jump capability, and without manipulators the U15 cannot grapple opponents or ride BattleMechs. Only a handful of these suits were assembled from battlefield salvage, making them exceedingly rare.

The Hauberk II is a close-combat adaptation of the Hauberk assault battle armor, developed for the Armed Forces of the Federated Suns during the Jihad. Produced by General Motors on Salem, the design replaced the base Hauberk's long-range armament with weapons better suited to urban fighting. Retaining the same heavy frame and defensive armor of its parent design, the Hauberk II gave AFFS infantry commanders a powerful option for the close-quarters engagements that defined the later stages of the conflict on New Avalon.

The Hauberk II trades the base model's long-range missile capability for close-quarters lethality. Twin Magshot Gauss Rifles replace the LRM-5, providing accurate, hard-hitting ballistic fire at short to medium ranges. A small pulse laser replaces the standard small laser, improving accuracy against fast-moving targets in the chaotic conditions of urban combat. The suit retains the improved stealth armor of its parent design, allowing troopers to close to effective range without drawing concentrated fire.

At two thousand kilograms, the Hauberk II shares the base model's movement limitations: ten kilometers per hour ground speed, no jump capability, and too heavy to ride OmniMechs. A battle claw provides close-combat capability. The design fills the same defensive role as the standard Hauberk but excels in enclosed environments where long-range weapons offer little advantage.

The Hauberk II emerged from the brutal urban fighting in Avalon City during the Word of Blake's occupation of New Avalon. Front-line AFFS troopers found the standard Hauberk's missile armament effectively useless in close confines, where engagement ranges rarely exceeded a few dozen meters. The suit's stealth protection also degraded in claw-to-claw engagements against Blakist Se'irim and Nephilim battle armor. Field technicians improvised a solution, salvaging compact ballistic weapons from fallen Cavalier suits to replace the missile system. This field-expedient refit addressed the short-range firepower gap and proved effective enough that General Motors on Salem soon began formal production of the modified design, supplying AFFS units fighting across the Federated Suns.

shared: The HeavyHauler is an industrial exoskeleton designed by General Motors for heavy cargo handling. Introduced in 3052 from GM's Kathil manufacturing complex, the 400-kilogram humanoid suit was purpose-built to give its operator exceptional lifting power in commercial and military logistics environments. Though not the first loader exoskeleton to reach the market, the HeavyHauler quickly became one of the most widely adopted, earning a reputation as a reliable workhorse across spaceports, warehouses, and DropShip loading bays throughout the Inner Sphere. GM's extensive manufacturing and distribution network ensured broad availability, making the design a natural choice for cartage companies and large-scale industrial operations.

The HeavyHauler is built around a single design principle: raw lifting power. Its paired cargo lifter manipulators can hoist a full two and a half metric tons and maneuver loads into precise positions, making it one of the most capable loader exoskeletons available. A cutting torch allows operators to open sealed containers and cut through packing materials, while an integrated searchlight supports work in poorly lit cargo holds and nighttime loading operations.

These advantages come at a cost. The suit moves at a slow walking pace, limiting its utility in time-sensitive logistics environments. More significantly, the HeavyHauler provides no armor protection beyond its basic structural frame, leaving operators exposed to workplace hazards. GM deliberately accepted these trade-offs to maximize the suit's carrying capacity within the 400-kilogram weight limit, producing a design that excels at sustained heavy lifting but demands careful operational planning to keep its operators safe.

General Motors brought the HeavyHauler to market not as the first loader exoskeleton, but as the most commercially successful. GM's reputation and extensive distribution network gave the design a decisive advantage over earlier, generic competitors. The company put the suit into active service at each of its factories, allowing potential customers to observe and test the design under realistic working conditions. This hands-on approach won GM numerous long-term purchase contracts and established the HeavyHauler's position as the industry standard.

Alongside Waytani's PowerLoader, the HeavyHauler became one of two benchmark designs in the loader exoskeleton market. Both suits featured proprietary lifter arm designs that competitors attempted to replicate, prompting GM and Waytani to pursue legal action in courts across the Free Worlds League and Federated Commonwealth. Judicial rulings consistently favored the original manufacturers, with significant damages awarded against imitators. Despite the emergence of newer loader designs, the HeavyHauler remained a common sight at transfer stations, spaceports, cargo vessels, and loading docks throughout the Inner Sphere.

shared: The Infiltrator was among the first battle armor designs fielded by any Inner Sphere military. Produced by Albion Advanced Technologies and Products on New Avalon, the light reconnaissance suit entered service in 3050 as a stealth-focused platform built around advanced sensor and concealment systems. Designed to operate deep behind enemy lines, the Infiltrator emphasized electronic stealth and intelligence-gathering capability over combat power, setting it apart from the heavier battle armor designs emerging across the Inner Sphere during the same period. The suit filled an important role in Federated Commonwealth force structure, providing covert reconnaissance capabilities that no other platform of its era could match.

The Infiltrator Mk. I is a 750-kilogram light battle armor suit built around stealth and sensor operations. Its 500 kilograms of prototype stealth armor incorporates radar, infrared, and acoustic suppression systems that mimic a combined ECM and IR sneak suit. This protection is minimal, absorbing roughly one hit from a medium laser before failing. The suit mounts an impressive array of passive sensing equipment, including heat sensors, magnetic-anomaly detectors, and recording devices capable of gathering intelligence deep within enemy territory. Its sole weapon is a heavy grenade launcher in the left arm, offering limited defensive firepower against unarmored personnel and light vehicles. A basic manipulator on the right arm provides object handling, though the suit is not configured for anti-BattleMech attacks or OmniMech transport. Ground speed reaches 21.6 km/h, but the suit's characteristic waddling stride and total lack of jump capability limit tactical mobility considerably.

The Infiltrator emerged from the early days of Inner Sphere battle armor development. When the first Clan technology samples reached the New Avalon Institute of Science during the opening years of the Clan Invasion, NAIS researchers recognized the potential for a lighter, more specialized battlesuit than the generalist Inner Sphere Standard then under parallel development. Drawing on captured salvage, the NAIS team created a reconnaissance platform that prioritized stealth and sensor capability over raw combat power. The result was one of the first two battle armor designs fielded by any Inner Sphere power, entering service alongside the Lyran Sloth in 3050.

The first prototype was dispatched to the 1st Somerset Strikers during their campaign against Clan Jade Falcon. Its initial combat test came during live-fire exercises on Waldorff V, when the renegade Falcon's Claws launched an unexpected attack. Fighting through swampy terrain that hampered its already limited mobility, the Infiltrator used mist cover and its concealment systems to hide from enemy forces and launch surprise attacks. The suit performed well enough to earn approval for full-scale production despite clear limitations.

Those limitations became painfully apparent as the Infiltrator reached frontline units in greater numbers. Operators quickly dubbed the suit the "Waddle" for its ungainly gait, and frustration mounted as commanders overestimated what it could accomplish and assigned it to missions far beyond its intended reconnaissance role. Sending a lightly protected stealth scout into direct engagements against standard battle armor produced predictable results. Yet operators who employed the Infiltrator within its design parameters found a different story. The suit could penetrate enemy lines undetected, position itself in observation posts no other platform could reach, and gather intelligence critical to operational planning.

The Infiltrator carved its deepest niche within Federated Commonwealth intelligence operations. The Federated Commonwealth Intelligence Command, along with DMI and MIIO field teams, recognized the suit's value for covert insertion and surveillance work. Purchases by intelligence agencies accounted for a significant share of early production. Thousands of suits were stationed across the Commonwealth by the time of the FedCom Civil War. Special forces operators who understood the suit's strengths proved it could infiltrate enemy territory, collect intelligence that no other platform could obtain, and deliver surprising lethality against soft targets before fading back into concealment.

The development of the superior Infiltrator Mk. II in 3060 gradually shifted frontline demand away from the original design. Production at Albion Advanced Technologies and Products on New Avalon wound down over the following decade, and the Mk. I line ceased production entirely by 3070. A second production line at TharHes Industries on Tharkad continued somewhat longer, serving Lyran Commonwealth demand. The suit remained in service well after production ended. AFFS and LAAF commanders who could not obtain enough Mk. II suits retained their Mk. I inventory, and covert operations units in both successor states maintained stockpiles for missions where the older suit's particular sensor profile remained useful.

The Special Ops configuration replaces the standard grenade launcher with an anti-personnel weapon mount for close-range defensive firepower. A remote sensor dispenser allows the operator to seed an area with monitoring devices and withdraw to a safe distance. Improved sensors and a laser microphone round out the surveillance suite, enabling the operator to detect concealed forces at greater range and eavesdrop on enemy communications. These modifications sacrifice what little offensive punch the baseline Infiltrator possesses, but intelligence operatives accept the trade for enhanced information-gathering capability. The suit retains the same prototype stealth armor and ground movement profile as the standard configuration, sharing its fragile protection and lack of jump capability.

shared: The Infiltrator Mk. II was developed by the New Avalon Institute of Science as a replacement for the original Infiltrator battle armor. Produced by Albion Advanced Technologies and Products on New Avalon, the medium-weight stealth suit entered service in 3060 after a lengthy development program. Nicknamed the "Puma" by its operators, the Mk. II addressed the shortcomings of its predecessor while preserving the core mission of deep reconnaissance and covert operations. The suit earned a strong reputation among Federated Commonwealth special forces and intelligence agencies as a capable platform for both stealth scouting and direct action missions that the original Infiltrator could not perform.

The Infiltrator Mk. II is a one-ton medium battle armor suit that pushes the stealth reconnaissance concept well beyond its predecessor's limits. Its primary weapon is a Federated-Barrett Magshot Gauss Rifle in the right arm, providing long-range precision fire well suited for sniping. An anti-personnel weapon mount in the left arm handles close-range engagements against enemy infantry. Both arms end in basic manipulators for anti-BattleMech attacks and OmniMech transport, though the right manipulator is encased within the weapon hardpoint when the Magshot is installed. Standard stealth armor weighing 360 kilograms provides protection against medium pulse laser fire while incorporating continuously recharged IR and ECM sneak suit capabilities. A personal ECM suite adds further electronic protection. Ground speed is a modest 10.8 km/h, but integral jump jets allow 90-meter leaps. An optional parafoil attachment enables high-altitude insertions for deep-penetration missions.

The Infiltrator Mk. II traces its origins to growing dissatisfaction with the original Infiltrator among Federated Commonwealth intelligence agencies. Though the Armed Forces of the Federated Commonwealth was the first Inner Sphere military to field battle armor, the sheer size of the AFFC worked against continued innovation. The Commonwealth had more line units to equip than any other nation and was still rebuilding formations shattered during the Clan Invasion. Research and development funding dropped as priority shifted toward recovering from battlefield losses, leaving new battle armor development stalled.

The Intelligence Secretariat, the command element of the Federated Commonwealth Intelligence Command, recognized the original Infiltrator's limitations most acutely. In February 3056, the Secretariat directed the Office of Science and Technology to coordinate with the NAIS on developing a replacement. Progress was slow until a breakthrough arrived from an unexpected source. In 3057, the Gray Death Legion discovered a Star League vault on Karbala containing several Mark XXI Nighthawk powered armor suits. Under orders from Archon-Prince Victor Steiner-Davion, Grayson Carlyle handed the recovered suits over to the NAIS, where they were systematically dismantled and analyzed. Though the Nighthawk suits were destroyed in the process, they provided invaluable data that accelerated the replacement program considerably. NAIS scientists began producing prototypes in January 3059, and full-scale production started in March 3060.

The resulting Mk. II quickly proved superior to its predecessor in nearly every measurable category except cost. Demand outstripped supply almost immediately. Both DMI and MIIO purchased close to forty percent of all suits manufactured in the early production runs. Losses during the FedCom Civil War further tightened an already strained supply chain, though the Puma could eventually be found in most Regimental Combat Teams and dedicated special forces units across both successor states.

The Mk. II's combat record established it as the premier Inner Sphere stealth battle armor. Covert operations forces praised its ability to scout enemy positions undetected and fight its way out when discovered. The suit remained in wide service across both the AFFS and LAAF after the FedCom schism, with commanders on both sides considering it essential equipment for special operations formations.

Several variant configurations emerged over the decades following initial production. A sensor-focused variant appeared in 3063, trading the primary weapon for enhanced detection equipment. During the Jihad, a magnetic clamp configuration entered service in 3071 for operators who needed to attach to vehicles or structures on the active battlefield. A marine variant designed for boarding operations followed in the Dark Age era. The experimental Coral Intent prototypes explored mimetic armor and C3 integration under Project CORAL INTENT at Achernar BattleMechs on New Avalon. Each configuration preserved the suit's core stealth characteristics while adapting mission equipment for specialized operational requirements. Production expanded beyond New Avalon when HDF Manufacturing on Falsterbo began manufacturing the standard Puma configuration during the late Republic era, ensuring continued supply as the political arena shifted across the former Federated Commonwealth.

Space operations adaptations allow the suit to function in vacuum environments, while magnetic clamps anchor the operator to ship hulls during extravehicular action. A cutting torch enables breaching sealed bulkheads and hatches. The standard Magshot is replaced with a Clan-manufactured micro pulse laser better suited to the tight confines of shipboard combat, where engagement ranges are measured in meters rather than hundreds of meters. The parafoil and anti-personnel weapon mount are removed to accommodate the specialized boarding equipment. The suit retains its stealth armor and ECM suite, making it difficult to detect during approach to a target vessel.

The Sensor configuration removes the Magshot Gauss Rifle to create a dedicated reconnaissance platform with enhanced detection capability. Improved sensors extend the operator's detection range and target identification accuracy. A machine gun on the right arm provides heavier anti-infantry firepower than the standard model, while a second anti-personnel weapon mount supplements close-range defense. This loadout is devastating against unarmored personnel but sacrifices the long-range precision strike capability that defines the standard Puma. The suit retains its stealth armor, ECM suite, jump jets, and parafoil compatibility, preserving the core infiltration mission while shifting the operator's role from precision shooter to area scout and infantry suppressor.

The Coral Intent is an experimental configuration developed under Project CORAL INTENT at Achernar BattleMechs on New Avalon. The prototypes replace the standard stealth armor with mimetic armor that adapts its surface appearance to surrounding terrain. A battle armor C3 system, acquired from Draconis Combine sources, provides networked targeting data to friendly units. Because the C3 system cannot function alongside the standard ECM suite, the Coral Intent trades electronic warfare protection for force multiplication through shared targeting. Federated-Barrett developed the "Thunderstick," a modification of the David light Gauss rifle, as the primary weapon after the standard Magshot proved too massive for the modified chassis. Basic manipulators on both arms and integral jump jets are retained. The prototypes remain in extended field testing, with operational deployment limited to evaluation scenarios.

The Ironhold is Clan Jade Falcon's dedicated assault battle armor, produced by Olivetti Weaponry on Sudeten. Entering service in 3077, the suit was developed during the Jihad as the Falcon response to the growing number of heavy and assault battle armor designs fielded by rival Clans and Inner Sphere powers. At two tons, the Ironhold balances firepower and protection while retaining greater agility than most assault-weight designs. Falcon warriors quickly embraced the suit for its combination of ranged lethality and tactical flexibility.

Developed after Falcon technicians received specifications for battle armor-scale LB-X autocannons, the Anti-Tank configuration replaces all Gauss weaponry with a pair of these weapons and a shoulder-mounted one-shot Inferno SRM launcher inspired by the Salamander battle armor. Like the Fire variant, the Anti-Tank model removes jump capability and uses fire-resistant armor. The autocannons give this configuration genuine anti-vehicle punch that the Gauss-armed models lack, while the Inferno launcher can overheat targets or ignite combustible materials. This loadout shifts the Ironhold's role from anti-infantry specialist to a vehicle hunter capable of threatening light combat vehicles and support assets. The configuration sacrifices sustained ammunition capacity for burst damage potential, making it dependent on careful engagement selection.

The Ironhold traces its origins to 3069, when Clan Jade Falcon's scientist caste began collaborating with Elementals from Gamma Galaxy to develop a new assault suit. The project, codenamed Ferrum, sought to combine assault-class protection with the mobility that Falcon warriors favored. An Elemental Trinary from the Third Falcon Talon Cluster was assigned to the program, accelerating development through direct warrior input. Prototype testing in the Periphery proved the design's combat potential, with results suggesting the Ironhold could supplant ProtoMechs in certain tactical roles.

Production delays pushed the Sudeten manufacturing line at Olivetti Weaponry to a 3077 activation date, years behind the original schedule. The newly manufactured suits saw immediate combat during the Coalition's advance on Shiloh that June. The suit spread rapidly across Jade Falcon Galaxies, with the Third Falcon Talon Cluster adopting it exclusively for all Elemental warriors. This concentrated deployment elevated the previously obscure Bang-Chu Elemental Bloodname to prominence within the Cluster.

The Fire configuration doubles the Ironhold's ranged firepower by mounting a second pair of Anti-Personnel Gauss Rifles on the suit's torso, bringing the total to four weapons with eighty rounds of combined ammunition. To accommodate the additional weaponry and the heavier fire-resistant armor that became standard on Jade Falcon battle armor, the jump jets were removed entirely. The bulk of the fireproof plating created stability issues that made safe jumping impossible. This trade sacrifices the standard model's mobility advantage but produces a dedicated close-assault platform with withering anti-infantry and anti-battle armor capability. The simplified construction allowed Olivetti Weaponry to manufacture the Fire variant faster than competing assault designs. Troopers must rely on ground speed and OmniMech transport to reach engagement range.

The standard Ironhold mounts two arm-mounted Anti-Personnel Gauss Rifles, each fed by a twenty-round magazine. These weapons provide excellent range and striking power against both infantry and light armored targets. The suit's two-ton frame carries sufficient standard armor to absorb considerable punishment, while integrated jump jets propel troopers up to sixty meters per bound. This mobility distinguishes the Ironhold from most assault-class battle armor, allowing operators to seize elevated positions and close gaps that heavier suits cannot. Battle claws on each arm enable swarming attacks against BattleMechs. The design trades raw firepower for tactical positioning, leaving it outgunned by dedicated fire-support suits in sustained engagements.

Developed by the New Avalon Institute of Science in the early 3050s, the Inner Sphere Standard was the first mass-produced battle armor fielded by the Great Houses. The medium-weight suit was reverse-engineered from captured Clan Elemental technology, giving Inner Sphere commanders their first viable counter to Clan powered infantry. Though inferior to its Clan counterpart in almost every measurable respect, the IS Standard proved reliable, affordable, and easy to manufacture across multiple production lines. Its widespread adoption reshaped Inner Sphere infantry doctrine, and the design served as the foundation for numerous successor suits developed by individual Great Houses and their defense contractors.

The Hive is a radical custom refit built for the "Four Myths and a Funeral" Gladiator team on Galatea. Advanced battle armor plating replaces the standard armor, and the right-arm modular weapon mount is removed in favor of an armored glove that allows conventional tool and weapon handling. A David light Gauss rifle is mounted in an underslung position beneath the left-arm battle claw, providing precision ranged firepower. The most significant modification is an experimental battle armor C3 system, likely salvaged from abandoned Word of Blake stores, that allows the Hive troopers to transmit targeting data to allied units including the team's modified Manticore. Jump jets are retained at standard capability. The C3 networking makes the Hive a powerful force multiplier, but the experimental technology and loss of modular weapon flexibility limit its utility outside the arena environment.

The Inner Sphere Standard battle armor traces its origins to the desperate months following Operation REVIVAL. When Clan forces struck the Inner Sphere in 3049, no Great House possessed powered infantry technology capable of matching the fearsome Elemental suits deployed by Clan warriors. Inner Sphere engineers initially had no battlefield salvage to study and were forced to consult fragmentary Star League records of early power armor programs like the Nighthawk. Early prototypes based on this limited data performed poorly in combat simulations.

The first battlefield victories against the Clans changed everything. Captured Elemental suits gave researchers at the New Avalon Institute of Science the breakthrough they needed. NAIS produced the first functional copies in 3050, and these early suits were immediately shipped to Federated Commonwealth units on the Clan front and select mercenary commands including the Gray Death Legion. Dubbed “gorilla suits” by the troops who wore them, these initial production models carried only half the armor of a Clan Elemental, lacked jump capability, and mounted a single modular weapon. Their performance against Clan opponents was mixed, but they proved that the Inner Sphere could field its own powered infantry.

Simultaneously, engineers in the Draconis Combine, Free Worlds League, and Capellan Confederation produced their own battle armor designs. That these independent programs yielded functionally identical suits has long been attributed to corporate espionage and illegal technology transfers across interstellar borders. Regardless of the cause, the rapid proliferation of manufacturing capacity across every major power transformed infantry warfare within just a few years.

Continuous refinement of the chassis corrected many early shortcomings. By the Battle of Tukayyid in 3052, the final production model incorporated compact jump jets, giving troopers the mobility to keep pace with BattleMech formations. Inner Sphere technological limitations still prevented the suit from matching the Elemental in raw capability, particularly the inability to combine jump capability with missile armament. These trade-offs were accepted as the cost of fielding powered infantry at scale.

The IS Standard’s greatest strength proved to be its accessibility. Manufacturers across every Great House produced the suit, and falling prices made it attractive to mercenary commands, private security firms, and even police forces. House Davion eventually transitioned its production lines entirely to the Cavalier, a cosmetically redesigned variant intended to boost AFFC morale following the Lyran secession. The Raiden served a similar purpose for the Draconis Combine. Despite these faction-specific replacements, IS Standard production continued in every other realm. The suit remained the most widely available battle armor design through the Jihad and well into the Dark Age.

By the thirty-second century, the IS Standard had become ubiquitous. Numerous manufacturers offered the suit to any buyer willing to place a bulk order, and several modernization programs extended the design’s combat relevance. Combine engineers developed a variant stripping the jump jets in favor of increased missile firepower, while Andurien workshops produced a field refit mimicking the capabilities of newer specialized designs. A further modernization leveraged advanced armor to incorporate magnetic clamps and improved jump capability. These ongoing updates ensured that the oldest Inner Sphere battle armor design remained competitive in a crowded market, decades after its initial fielding.
