shared: The flamer-equipped IS Standard provides close-range area denial against conventional infantry and light defensive positions. The suit mounts a single flamer in its right-arm modular weapon slot, complemented by a left-arm battle claw for anti-BattleMech swarming attacks and OmniMech transport handholds. Standard armor plating absorbs moderate punishment, sufficient to keep a trooper alive through a full burst from a large pulse laser. Compact jump jets allow troopers to cover ninety meters per bound, maintaining pace with mechanized formations. The flamer configuration excels at clearing entrenched infantry from buildings and fortifications, but its complete inability to damage armored vehicles or BattleMechs beyond point-blank swarming range limits the loadout to dedicated anti-personnel operations.

The small laser configuration gives the IS Standard a versatile energy weapon requiring no ammunition resupply. The right-arm modular mount carries a single small laser capable of threatening light vehicles and conventional infantry at moderate range. The left-arm battle claw allows anti-BattleMech attacks and OmniMech transport capability. Standard armor protection and ninety-meter jump capability remain unchanged from other configurations. The laser loadout's greatest advantage is sustained engagement capability, as troopers need not worry about ammunition depletion during extended operations or prolonged patrols far from supply lines. Its primary weakness is limited damage output, insufficient to threaten heavily armored targets through direct fire alone.

Fielded beginning in 3061 during the Capellan-St. Ives War, the light recoilless rifle configuration offers a balanced anti-personnel and light anti-armor capability. The right-arm modular mount carries a single light recoilless rifle with enough penetration to damage light vehicles while remaining effective against infantry. The left-arm battle claw enables swarming attacks and mechanized transport. Standard armor and ninety-meter jump capability are unchanged. The recoilless rifle provides better range and harder-hitting rounds than the machine gun loadout, making it effective against a wider variety of targets. Ammunition is limited, however, and the weapon lacks the sustained fire capability of the machine gun or the unlimited endurance of the small laser.

shared: The Magnetic modernization trades the IS Standard's traditional armor for lighter advanced plating, freeing mass for magnetic clamps and a jump booster system. Magnetic clamps allow the suit to ride on the exterior of friendly BattleMechs and vehicles without requiring OmniMech-style handholds, solving a persistent transport challenge for Inner Sphere battle armor formations. The jump booster extends leap distance to one hundred twenty meters per bound, a marked improvement in tactical mobility. A single machine gun provides anti-infantry firepower, while the left-arm battle claw enables swarming attacks. Inspired by a similar Longinus variant, the Magnetic sacrifices armor protection for mobility and transport flexibility. The thinner plating leaves troopers more exposed to concentrated fire than the standard model.

The machine gun configuration makes the IS Standard a devastating anti-personnel platform. The right-arm modular mount carries a single machine gun delivering sustained automatic fire against conventional infantry and unarmored targets. The left-arm battle claw provides anti-BattleMech capability and OmniMech transport handholds. Standard armor and ninety-meter jump jets give the suit adequate survivability and tactical mobility across most terrain types. The machine gun's high rate of fire makes this configuration lethal against soft targets in open terrain, but its rounds are wholly ineffective against armored vehicles and BattleMech-grade plating. Ammunition dependence also limits the duration of sustained engagements compared to energy weapon loadouts.

The SRM configuration gives the IS Standard its only dedicated anti-armor loadout among the original weapon options. A single one-shot SRM-2 launcher occupies the right-arm modular mount, providing enough punch to threaten BattleMech armor at close range. The left-arm battle claw complements this with swarming attack capability. Standard armor protection keeps the trooper alive through moderate fire. However, this configuration carries a significant tactical penalty: Inner Sphere technology cannot combine jump jets with mounted missile launchers, forcing troopers to choose between mobility and firepower. Once the missiles are expended, the suit retains only its battle claw for offensive capability, making the SRM loadout a calculated gamble rather than a sustained fighting option.

text.overview: The Gray Death Heavy Suit is a heavy battle armor design produced by Defiance Industries on Furillo. Introduced in 3083, the suit was the first entirely new Gray Death design created after Defiance absorbed Gray Death Technologies. Built for direct assault operations where lighter suits lack the necessary firepower, the Heavy carries significantly heavier weaponry and armor than other designs in the Gray Death family, filling the heavy fire support role within Lyran battle armor formations.
text.capabilities:
The Gray Death Heavy Suit is the largest and most heavily armed design in the Gray Death battle armor family. A built-in Support PPC provides sustained direct-fire capability against armored targets, while two detachable one-shot SRM-4 packs deliver a devastating opening salvo. A Basic Manipulator and Improved Sensors round out the equipment package. At 1,500 kilograms, the suit carries significantly more armor than its lighter siblings.

Ground speed tops out at 21 km/h, making the Heavy the slowest Gray Death design. The suit lacks jump capability entirely, limiting its tactical mobility in broken terrain. The trade-off is raw combat power: the Support PPC can threaten targets that lighter battle armor cannot meaningfully engage, and the twin SRM-4 packs allow a single trooper to deliver concentrated missile fire before closing to direct-fire range. Once the missile packs are expended and jettisoned, the trooper relies on the Support PPC alone.
text.deployment: Six-trooper Level I formations of Gray Death Heavy Suits delivered devastating opening salvos when all twelve detachable missile packs fired simultaneously. Com Guard doctrine leveraged the Heavy's firepower in defensive operations, positioning Level I units at chokepoints where the suit's limited mobility was less of a disadvantage. The additional troopers compensated for the Heavy's slow speed by providing overlapping fields of fire that could cover a wider frontage than a four-trooper squad.
text.battleHistory:
The Gray Death Heavy Suit entered production at the Defiance Industries plant on Furillo in 3083, the first entirely new Gray Death design created after Defiance absorbed Gray Death Technologies. Where the Scout, Standard, and Strike Suits all traced their lineage to the original Gray Death Legion, the Heavy was a Defiance product from inception. Designed for direct assault rather than the combined-arms flexibility of earlier Gray Death armor, the 1,500-kilogram suit carried substantially heavier weaponry and protection than its predecessors.

Production began during the early Republic era as the Lyran Commonwealth rebuilt military capacity lost during the Jihad. The Heavy filled a gap in the LCAF's battle armor inventory, providing a platform capable of engaging hardened targets that lighter Gray Death suits could not threaten effectively. Defiance marketed the suit alongside the Standard and Scout as part of a complete Gray Death battle armor family, offering LCAF commanders complementary light, medium, and heavy options from a single manufacturer.

text.deployment: LCAF commanders fielded four-trooper squads of the anti-infantry configuration for general-purpose operations where both armored and unarmored threats were expected. The dual-weapon loadout gave squad leaders tactical options against a wide range of targets without requiring mission-specific reconfigurations. Lyran garrison regiments stationed along contested borders adopted this loadout as their default Infiltrator configuration, valuing its balanced capability over the specialized alternatives.

Five-trooper Clan Points operating the anti-infantry configuration gained a medium battle armor element suited to both offensive and defensive operations. The combination of ranged and close-quarters firepower allowed Points to engage mixed opposition without relying on external support. Clan garrison commanders who acquired the suits deployed them alongside heavier assets as a flexible screening force capable of handling unarmored and lightly armored threats alike.

Six-trooper Level I formations with the anti-infantry configuration provided Com Guard and successor organizations with a well-rounded infantry element. The larger formation amplified the loadout's balanced firepower, allowing Level I commanders to assign fire teams against separate target types simultaneously. Republic of the Sphere forces inherited some of these formations during the transition from ComStar military operations.

LCAF engineers employed four-trooper squads of the mine-laying configuration to prepare defensive positions and deny enemy approach routes. Inserted covertly ahead of an expected attack, these squads seeded chokepoints and likely avenues of advance before withdrawing to friendly lines. Lyran defensive doctrine emphasized channeling enemy formations into prepared kill zones, and the Infiltrator's stealth insertion capability made it ideal for emplacing obstacles without alerting the opposition.

Five-trooper Clan Points configured for area denial deployed mines along approaches to garrison installations and supply depots. The additional trooper expanded the area that each Point could seed during a single sortie. Clan commanders who valued defensive preparation over aggressive maneuver found the configuration useful for securing rear areas against raiding forces and insurgent activity on occupied worlds.

Six-trooper Level I formations with mine-laying capability could deny larger areas than smaller formations, establishing obstacle belts that forced attackers into predictable avenues of approach. Com Guard defensive planners integrated these formations into layered defense schemes, using the mine-equipped troopers to shape the battlefield before heavier assets engaged. The stealthy insertion method allowed obstacles to appear where the enemy least expected them.

LCAF signals intelligence units employed four-trooper squads of the remote sensor configuration to establish unattended surveillance networks. Squads inserted into an area, deployed their sensor packages along enemy supply routes or around high-value targets, and withdrew before detection. The resulting sensor network continued feeding data back to command long after the troopers had moved on, providing persistent intelligence coverage without risking personnel.

Five-trooper Clan Points carrying autonomous surveillance packages established early warning networks around Clan-held installations and defensive perimeters. The additional trooper allowed each Point to seed sensors across a wider area in a single operation. Clan Watch operatives occasionally employed these Points for covert surveillance of rival Clan movements during periods of inter-Clan tension, exploiting the Infiltrator's stealth characteristics to avoid detection.

Six-trooper Level I formations configured for remote sensor deployment could blanket an entire sector with autonomous detection devices in a single sortie. Com Guard commanders used these formations to establish sensor fences along planetary approaches and around critical infrastructure. The unattended sensors provided continuous surveillance without tying down combat personnel, freeing Level I formations to redeploy once their sensor packages were in place.

LCAF intelligence officers assigned four-trooper squads of the sensor-enhanced configuration to deep reconnaissance missions behind enemy lines. Inserted by aerial drop, these squads mapped enemy force dispositions, identified command nodes, and tracked reinforcement movements before withdrawing to friendly lines. The Lyran preference for thorough pre-battle intelligence made this configuration a priority asset for regimental and brigade-level commanders planning offensive operations.

Five-trooper Clan Points carrying enhanced sensor packages served as the eyes of garrison clusters on contested worlds. The expanded Point size allowed commanders to maintain overlapping sensor coverage across multiple approaches to defended positions. Clan doctrine traditionally relied on heavier assets for reconnaissance, but the Infiltrator's stealth profile offered detection capabilities that OmniMechs could not replicate without exposing themselves to enemy observation.

Six-trooper Level I formations optimized for sensor operations provided Com Guard commanders with dedicated intelligence-gathering elements at the tactical level. The larger formation could cover more ground than smaller squads, establishing a comprehensive sensor picture across an entire sector. These formations typically operated well forward of the main defensive line, providing early warning of enemy movements and feeding data back to command posts in near-real time.

LCAF combined-arms formations paired four-trooper squads of the designation configuration with artillery batteries and units carrying guided munitions. Squads inserted ahead of the main force via aerial drop, using the suit's low observability to reach designation range undetected. Lyran commanders valued these squads for breaking open fortified positions that direct-fire assets could not reduce efficiently.

Five-trooper Clan Points equipped for target designation extended their formation's ability to coordinate indirect fire across a wider engagement area. Clan garrison forces paired these Points with artillery Stars, using the Infiltrator's stealth characteristics to position designators where enemy counter-battery fire could not easily reach them. The fifth trooper provided additional redundancy for a mission where losing a single designator could collapse the entire fire support plan.

Six-trooper Level I formations configured for target designation gave Com Guard commanders multiple simultaneous designation points across a battlefront. The additional troopers allowed Level I leaders to maintain continuous designation coverage even as individual troopers repositioned or came under fire. This redundancy proved critical during defensive operations where artillery support was the primary means of breaking enemy advances.

The Reaper configuration saw service with LAAF and mercenary squads that needed their Scout troopers to carry more firepower into the field. Four-trooper squads armed with Clan-manufactured weapons could handle ambush situations and chance contacts without calling for reinforcement, addressing a common complaint about the unarmed base Scout. Mercenary commands operating along the Periphery border found the Reaper particularly useful for independent patrol operations where support was hours away.

Five-trooper Clan Points fielding the Reaper configuration gained a scouting element with genuine offensive teeth. The Clan-manufactured weapons fitted naturally into Clan logistics chains, simplifying maintenance and ammunition supply compared to the base Scout's reliance on hand-carried Inner Sphere small arms. Points operating the Reaper typically screened for heavier formations, engaging targets of opportunity while feeding sensor data back to the main body.

Six-trooper Level I formations equipped with the Reaper configuration combined the Scout's stealth and sensor advantages with enough organic firepower to contest enemy reconnaissance screens. The additional two troopers over a standard Inner Sphere squad gave Level I Reaper teams greater staying power in running engagements. Com Guard doctrine emphasized using these formations to establish forward sensor networks while denying the same capability to opposing forces.

Inner Sphere commanders organized Gray Death Scout troopers into four-trooper squads following standard infantry doctrine. The Gray Death Legion fielded its Scout Suits in dedicated reconnaissance squads that operated ahead of the main force, mapping enemy positions and identifying weaknesses in defensive lines. After the Legion's destruction, LAAF units adopted the same squad structure, pairing Scout squads with Gray Death Standard squads for combined light and medium battle armor operations. Scout squads proved especially effective in wooded and urban terrain where their enhanced sensors could locate concealed enemies that heavier units would walk into blind.

Clan Points of five troopers occasionally fielded captured or salvaged Gray Death Scout Suits, particularly among second-line and garrison formations where procurement of front-line Elemental armor was not prioritized. The Scout's sensor capabilities and stealth characteristics appealed to Clan commanders who needed reconnaissance assets without committing Elemental Points to scouting duties. Five-trooper Points expanded the sensor coverage that each formation could maintain across a wider front.

ComStar and Word of Blake formations organized Gray Death Scout Suits into six-trooper Level I units. The additional troopers allowed Level I commanders to split their formation into paired fire teams while maintaining continuous sensor coverage. Com Guard units valued the Scout's intelligence-gathering capability for supporting their doctrine of information superiority on the battlefield. Word of Blake Militia formations that acquired the suits used them in a similar fashion during the Jihad.

LAAF and mercenary commands fielded four-trooper squads of the Standard Suit's incendiary configuration for urban operations and close-quarters fighting. The weapon's area-effect properties made these squads particularly effective at clearing buildings and flushing defenders from prepared positions. Gray Death Legion veterans favored this loadout for operations on densely forested worlds where conventional infantry could hide in terrain that BattleMechs could not easily search.

Clan Points fielding captured Standard Suits with incendiary weapons employed them in garrison roles where area denial mattered more than ranged precision. Five troopers equipped for close-range engagements could control corridors, intersections, and chokepoints that heavier assets would overcommit to holding. Second-line formations found the configuration adequate for suppressing unarmored resistance on occupied worlds.

Six-trooper Level I formations with incendiary loadouts served Com Guard and Word of Blake commands in area denial and counter-insurgency operations. The additional troopers allowed Level I commanders to establish overlapping zones of control in confined spaces. Word of Blake Militia units deployed these formations during the occupation of contested worlds, where suppressing civilian resistance demanded persistent presence in urban centers.

The energy weapon configuration became the most widely issued Standard Suit loadout among LAAF regular formations. Four-trooper squads appreciated the freedom from ammunition dependency during extended operations where resupply was uncertain. LAAF doctrine paired these squads with BattleMech lances for combined-arms operations, using the troopers to secure flanks, clear buildings, and exploit gaps that 'Mechs created in enemy lines.

Com Guard Level I formations favored the energy weapon configuration for its sustained engagement capability. Six troopers maintaining continuous fire without ammunition concerns gave Level I commanders reliable suppressive capability during protracted defensive actions. ComStar's emphasis on holding ground until reinforcement arrived made the configuration's endurance more valuable than the heavier hitting power of alternative loadouts.

The ballistic rifle configuration entered LAAF service later than the original four weapon options, and four-trooper squads carrying this loadout were less common as a result. Commanders who fielded them valued the weapon's effective range and versatility against mixed target types. LAAF units operating along the former Free Worlds League border found the configuration well suited to the raiding and counter-raiding operations that characterized the post-Jihad security environment.

Clan Points equipped with the ballistic rifle configuration gained a versatile ranged engagement option that appealed to commanders who needed flexibility over specialization. Five troopers with effective anti-armor reach could engage a wider range of targets than Points carrying weapons optimized for a single role. The configuration's later introduction date meant fewer captured suits reached Clan hands compared to the original four loadouts.

Six-trooper Level I formations with the ballistic rifle configuration provided balanced firepower effective against both armored and soft targets. The weapon's range advantage over most other Standard Suit options allowed Level I commanders to engage at distances where enemy infantry could not effectively return fire. Com Guard units deployed these formations in open-terrain defensive positions where standoff distance was more valuable than the close-quarters capability of other loadouts.

Four-trooper squads carrying the high-volume ballistic loadout excelled at anti-infantry operations. LAAF commanders assigned these squads to sectors where conventional enemy troops were the primary threat, freeing heavier assets for armored engagements. Mercenary commands operating in counter-insurgency campaigns found the configuration cost-effective for sustained patrol and security operations where most contacts involved unarmored opponents.

Five-trooper Clan Points equipped with the ballistic configuration typically drew garrison and rear-area security assignments. The weapon's effectiveness against conventional infantry made it well suited to maintaining order on occupied worlds, a duty that frontline warriors considered beneath them. Solahma and second-line warriors assigned to these Points accepted the role as necessary, if unglamorous, service to the Clan.

Six-trooper Level I formations with high-volume ballistic weapons provided effective anti-infantry screening for Com Guard and Word of Blake commands. The additional troopers delivered concentrated firepower that could shred conventional infantry formations caught in the open. Word of Blake Militia units deployed these formations extensively during planetary occupation operations where suppressing armed civilian resistance was a daily requirement.

LAAF assault planners designated four-trooper squads carrying the missile loadout as priority anti-armor assets within battle armor platoons. These squads received specific target assignments during combined-arms operations, engaging light vehicles and exposed BattleMech components at ranges beyond what close-combat weapons could reach. Careful ammunition management was drilled into every trooper, as expending all four rounds without achieving a mission-critical result left the squad dependent on secondary weapons.

Five-trooper Clan Points carrying the missile configuration brought respectable anti-armor capability to second-line formations that lacked dedicated heavy battle armor. The concentrated salvo from a full Point could threaten light OmniMechs and armored vehicles that lighter weapons could not meaningfully damage. Clan commanders treated these Points as a supplementary fire support element, committing them against specific hardened targets rather than general infantry engagements.

Six-trooper Level I formations with missile loadouts delivered the heaviest single-volley firepower available from Gray Death Standard Suits. Com Guard commanders held these formations in reserve for decisive moments, deploying them against armored targets that lighter configurations could not threaten. The larger formation size partially offset the limited ammunition supply, as the combined salvo from six troopers could cripple most light vehicles in a single coordinated strike.

LCAF commands operating in hostile atmospheric or vacuum conditions adopted the self-sealing variant for four-trooper squads tasked with boarding actions and operations on worlds with hazardous environments. The suit's ability to maintain integrity after armor breaches gave troopers confidence in situations where a single puncture could prove fatal. Lyran naval infantry units were among the first to receive the variant for shipboard assault operations.

Five-trooper Clan Points equipped with the self-sealing variant found use in hostile environment operations that other battle armor could not safely undertake. Garrison clusters defending installations on worlds with corrosive or toxic atmospheres valued the suit's ability to maintain atmospheric integrity under fire. The additional trooper provided redundancy for operations where evacuation of a wounded trooper was complicated by environmental hazards.

Six-trooper Level I formations of the self-sealing variant provided Com Guard and successor organizations with battle armor capable of sustained operations in environments that would incapacitate conventionally sealed suits. The larger formation size allowed Level I commanders to rotate troopers through hazardous exposure zones while maintaining combat effectiveness. These formations saw particular value during boarding operations and planetary assaults against defended installations with compromised atmospherics.

Five-trooper Clan Points operating prototype Strike Suits would have benefited from the Clan-manufactured launcher system that integrated naturally with Clan logistics chains. The prototype's superior reach and hitting power compared to the production model made it an attractive acquisition for Clan garrison forces, though the extreme rarity of these experimental suits limited any organized Clan deployment to captured or salvaged examples.

Six-trooper Level I formations of prototype Strike Suits existed only in theory, as the small number of prototypes produced never reached ComStar or Word of Blake hands in sufficient quantity for organized formation-level deployment. Any Level I equipped with these experimental suits would have gained substantial fire support capability from the Clan-sourced weapon systems, but the prototypes remained confined to their original operators throughout their limited service life.

Defiance Industries sold the production Strike Suit exclusively to the Lyran Commonwealth, and LCAF commanders organized them into four-trooper fire support squads. These squads advanced behind scout and assault elements, delivering missile volleys against hardened targets identified by forward observers. After expending their ordnance, troopers shifted to a designation role, guiding friendly artillery and guided munitions onto enemy positions. LCAF units operating along the former Free Worlds League border employed Strike squads extensively in raiding operations.

Five-trooper Clan Points fielding the production Strike Suit gained a dedicated fire support element that complemented heavier assault armor. The additional trooper increased each Point's total missile output, giving garrison cluster commanders a meaningful indirect fire capability at the battle armor level. The suit's lack of jump capability limited its appeal to Clan warriors accustomed to more mobile platforms, confining it primarily to defensive and garrison assignments.

Six-trooper Level I formations of the production Strike Suit concentrated enough missile firepower to threaten light vehicles and exposed BattleMech components in coordinated salvos. Com Guard successors deployed these formations in prepared defensive positions where the suit's ground-only movement was less of a liability. The additional troopers ensured that even after some had expended their ordnance, the formation retained enough designators to maintain fire support coordination.

The C3-networked Hunter-Killer configuration entered service with AFFS formations that had adopted battalion-level C3 networks during the Dark Age. Four-trooper squads link into the network as forward fire nodes, sharing targeting data that improves accuracy for all connected units. The Robinson Rangers integrated these squads into their combined arms doctrine, positioning them as flanking elements where the network link compensated for the squad's reduced individual firepower compared to missile-armed Hunter-Killer variants.

Augmented five-trooper C3 Hunter-Killer squads maximize the network's force multiplication effect by adding another data node to the formation. The Federated Suns Armored Cavalry adopted the five-suit configuration for its reconnaissance battle armor platoons, where the C3 link fed targeting data back to following armored formations in real time. The additional trooper also provides security for the squad during the vulnerable moments when operators focus on network coordination rather than local threats.

Six-trooper C3 Hunter-Killer formations provide redundant network nodes across a wider frontage than smaller squads can cover. These reinforced teams are fielded by AFFS commands that rely heavily on networked fire coordination, particularly in defensive operations where the C3 link enables supporting units to engage targets designated by forward-positioned battle armor. The Draconis March organized oversized C3 squads for border defense, where sustained network coverage across extended defensive lines justified the additional manpower commitment.

The variable speed pulse laser and Magshot combination entered AFFS service during the Dark Age as a sustained-fire alternative to the missile-armed Hunter-Killer variants. Four-trooper squads carrying this loadout deploy with formations that expect extended engagements without reliable resupply. The Davion Brigade of Guards adopted the configuration for its battle armor company, valuing the energy weapon's unlimited ammunition as insurance against the logistical disruptions that plagued AFFS operations during the Fortress Republic period.

Five-trooper squads with the pulse laser and Magshot loadout see service in AFFS commands that operate independently for extended periods. The Syrtis Fusiliers fielded augmented squads of this configuration along the Capellan border, where the mixed energy and ballistic weapons gave troopers sustained combat capability without the ammunition constraints that limited purely projectile-armed formations. The additional trooper provides the squad with greater flexibility to split into fire teams during complex engagements.

Reinforced six-trooper squads carrying the pulse laser and Magshot combination are uncommon, fielded primarily by AFFS garrison commands concerned with sustained defensive capability. The Kilbourne PDZ militia organized oversized squads of this configuration for perimeter defense operations, where the energy weapon's endurance advantage over purely ammunition-dependent loadouts allowed troopers to maintain continuous fire during prolonged sieges without the resupply requirements that would have strained the militia's limited logistics chain.

The standard four-trooper Grenadier squad is the most common formation fielded by AFFS line units. Mechanized infantry battalions attached to Regimental Combat Teams typically deploy these squads in pairs, with one squad providing missile suppression while the other closes to laser range. The Syrtis Fusiliers and Davion Assault Guards both maintain significant inventories of the standard configuration, relying on its balanced firepower for urban security and garrison duties along the Capellan border.

Five-trooper squads operating the standard configuration appear in augmented battle armor companies where additional manpower is available. The extra trooper provides redundancy against casualties while increasing the squad's total missile output. Several March Militia formations along the Draconis border adopted the five-suit formation after the Jihad, finding that the additional firepower compensated for the Grenadier's limited protection when facing Combine raiding forces that favored fast strikes against fixed positions.

Reinforced six-trooper squads carrying the standard loadout are rare outside of dedicated assault formations. The Ceti Hussars experimented with oversized Grenadier squads during anti-piracy operations in the Periphery March, concluding that the concentrated missile fire from six suits could suppress BattleMech-scale targets long enough for supporting armor to close. The formation demands significant transport capacity and is generally reserved for operations where overwhelming close-range firepower justifies the logistical burden.

Configuration A serves as the general-purpose combat loadout for AFFS units fielding the Grenadier II. Four-trooper squads are the standard formation, deployed by elite commands that have access to the mixed-technology suit. The First Davion Guards were among the earliest AFFS recipients, integrating the Mk. II into their existing battle armor doctrine as a lighter complement to the original Grenadier. The suit's ability to ride OmniMechs gave these squads tactical mobility that the heavier original could not match.

Five-trooper squads of Configuration A appear in augmented AFFS battle armor companies attached to frontline RCTs. The Davion Assault Guards adopted the five-suit formation to maximize the Grenadier II's OmniMech transport capability, fitting extra troopers onto available carrying capacity. The additional suit increases squad-level missile output while providing casualty redundancy during extended mechanized operations where replacement troopers are unavailable.

Reinforced six-trooper squads operating Configuration A are rare and generally limited to garrison formations that have received surplus Grenadier II suits from frontline commands. The Crucis March Militia assembled oversized squads for planetary defense exercises, finding that the additional firepower offset the militia troopers' lower proficiency with the suit's mixed-technology systems, particularly the Clan-sourced components that demanded more skilled maintenance than standard AFFS equipment.

Configuration B squads serve as networked indirect fire platforms within AFFS C3-equipped formations. Standard four-trooper teams typically attach to combined arms companies where the long-range missile capability complements direct-fire assets. The Robinson Rangers integrated Configuration B squads into their reconnaissance screen, where the C3 link fed targeting data to following armored columns while the troopers contributed long-range missile fire from concealed positions.

Augmented five-trooper Configuration B squads maximize the C3 network's coverage by adding another data node to the formation. The Federated Suns Armored Cavalry fielded five-suit teams in its forward reconnaissance elements, where the additional trooper provided security while the squad focused on network coordination and target designation. The long-range missile loadout allowed these squads to contribute meaningful firepower without abandoning their observation positions.

Six-trooper Configuration B formations provide sustained C3 network coverage across extended frontages. These oversized squads are organized by AFFS commands that rely on networked fire coordination for defensive operations, particularly along the Draconis border where Combine raiding tactics demand early warning and rapid fire response. The reinforced squad ensures that network coverage persists even after casualties reduce the formation below standard strength.

Configuration C equips the Grenadier II for close-to-medium range energy combat, and four-trooper squads are the standard formation for AFFS commands operating in environments where ammunition resupply is unreliable. The Syrtis Fusiliers adopted Configuration C for operations in the contested worlds along the Capellan border, where the all-energy loadout freed logistical capacity for other formations. The OmniMech transport capability allows these squads to rapidly redeploy between engagement areas without dedicated transport vehicles.

Five-trooper Configuration C squads deliver concentrated energy firepower in sustained engagements. The augmented formation sees service with AFFS units conducting extended operations in remote areas, where the ammunition independence of the all-energy loadout proves decisive. Several Periphery March garrison commands fielded five-suit Configuration C teams for anti-bandit patrols, where the squads could operate for weeks without resupply convoys that would reveal patrol routes to hostile forces.

Reinforced six-trooper Configuration C formations concentrate overwhelming energy firepower for deliberate assault operations. These oversized squads are uncommon and typically assembled for specific missions requiring sustained close-range combat capability. The Ceti Hussars organized reinforced Configuration C teams for urban clearance exercises, concluding that the massed thermal and laser output could suppress defenders in fortified positions long enough for supporting infantry to secure the objective.

Configuration D is exclusive to Republic of the Sphere forces, and standard four-trooper squads formed the backbone of RAF battle armor artillery sections. The Republic acquired the Grenadier II through clandestine channels via Republic-friendly agencies in the Federated Suns, reserving this configuration for its own forces. RAF commanders paired Configuration D squads with Grenadier II units in other loadouts, creating self-contained battle armor formations with organic indirect fire support that did not rely on external artillery assets.

Augmented five-trooper Configuration D squads provided the RAF with enhanced indirect fire capability at the squad level. The Republic employed these formations for covert operations beyond the Fortress walls, where the Davion-manufactured suits helped mask Republic involvement in border raids. The additional trooper increased the squad's sustained bombardment capacity and provided local security during fire missions, when operators focused on artillery calculations rather than perimeter awareness.

Six-trooper Configuration D formations represented the Republic's heaviest organic battle armor artillery capability. These reinforced squads were assembled for deliberate bombardment missions where sustained indirect fire was required. RAF commanders on Marlette reportedly employed oversized Configuration D teams to confuse Capellan intelligence about the source of artillery fire during border operations, as the self-supporting suits left no vehicle-scale signatures for enemy sensors to identify as conventional artillery positions.

Inner Sphere military commands that adopted the Groundhog typically organized Armored Glove operators into four-trooper squads, following standard infantry doctrine. These squads served as combat engineering support elements attached to BattleMech or conventional armor formations, providing field security and light anti-BattleMech capability alongside their engineering duties. The Armored Glove configuration's ability to handle infantry weapons made it the preferred choice for squads operating in contested environments where engineering teams might face direct contact.

Clan formations that acquired Groundhog exoskeletons through salvage or trade organized operators into five-trooper Points, consistent with standard Clan military structure. The Armored Glove configuration saw limited Clan adoption given the generally low regard for industrial exoskeletons among warrior caste personnel, but labor and garrison castes occasionally fielded Points for facility defense and engineering support where dedicated Elemental suits were unavailable or unwarranted.

ComStar and Word of Blake forces organized Groundhog operators into six-trooper Level I formations. The Word of Blake's occupation of Solaris VII beginning in 3068 gave their forces direct access to Blue Shot Weapons' remaining inventory, and Armored Glove-equipped Level Is provided the Blakists with engineering and light security capability in the contested urban environment of Solaris City's arena districts.

Inner Sphere squads equipped with Basic Manipulator Groundhogs filled a general-purpose engineering role within combined arms formations. Four-trooper squads handled field repairs, equipment setup, and logistics support tasks that required more dexterity than brute strength. The configuration's retained combat capability made it a practical choice for militia and mercenary units that needed flexible engineering support without dedicating separate security elements.

Clan Points fielding Basic Manipulator Groundhogs served primarily in rear-area support roles, performing maintenance and logistics tasks at garrison facilities. The exoskeleton's general-purpose manipulators suited the broad range of duties assigned to Clan labor caste personnel, and five-trooper Points could cover substantial work areas during facility maintenance rotations.

Word of Blake and ComStar Level I formations equipped with Basic Manipulator Groundhogs served as general engineering support within garrison commands. Six-trooper formations provided sufficient personnel to handle field maintenance, communications equipment setup, and logistics coordination tasks. The configuration saw common assignment to Militia units tasked with infrastructure support during the Jihad.

Inner Sphere logistics commands organized Cargo Lifter Groundhogs into four-trooper squads for forward supply operations. Each squad could move up to four tons of materiel simultaneously, dramatically accelerating ammunition resupply and equipment redistribution in the field. These squads proved popular with mercenary units operating without dedicated logistics vehicles, filling a critical gap in light formation support structures.

Clan labor caste personnel operating Cargo Lifter Groundhogs in five-trooper Points handled supply distribution and equipment transport at Clan garrison facilities. The one-ton-per-suit lifting capacity made Points of Cargo Lifter Groundhogs efficient alternatives to heavier cargo handling equipment in facilities where vehicle access was restricted or impractical.

ComStar and Word of Blake Level I formations equipped with Cargo Lifter Groundhogs supported logistics operations at HPG compounds and military depots. Six-trooper formations provided substantial combined lifting capacity for resupply operations, and the Blakist garrison on Solaris VII made particular use of these formations during the occupation to redistribute captured military supplies.

Inner Sphere combat engineering squads equipped with Industrial Drill Groundhogs specialized in rapid fortification construction, obstacle clearance, and demolition preparation. Four-trooper squads could establish defensive positions or cut through reinforced barriers significantly faster than unaugmented sappers. Lyran Alliance engineering battalions and mercenary commands operating along the Periphery border showed the strongest interest in this configuration.

Clan Points operating Industrial Drill Groundhogs served in construction and mining roles at Clan garrison worlds and industrial facilities. Five-trooper Points provided efficient excavation and drilling capability for infrastructure projects, and the configuration's rugged design suited the demanding conditions found on many Clan occupation zone worlds.

Word of Blake engineering formations organized Industrial Drill Groundhogs into six-trooper Level Is for fortification and infrastructure projects. During the occupation of Solaris VII, Blakist engineers used these formations to construct defensive positions throughout the arena districts and to clear debris from battle-damaged areas of Solaris City.

Inner Sphere military commands organized Mine Clearance Groundhogs into four-trooper squads tasked with route clearance and area denial countermeasures. These squads typically operated ahead of advancing formations, clearing paths through minefields that would otherwise require slower conventional disposal methods. The suit's armor provided meaningfully better protection for disposal technicians than standard bomb disposal gear.

Clan Points equipped with Mine Clearance Groundhogs addressed a capability gap that most Clan Toumans had historically neglected. Clan doctrine emphasized offensive action over defensive measures, leaving minefield clearance to lower-caste support personnel. Five-trooper Points of Mine Clearance Groundhogs provided garrison forces with a practical solution for securing territories where retreating enemies had laid defensive minefields.

ComStar and Word of Blake Level I formations fielded Mine Clearance Groundhogs for route clearance and security operations. The Word of Blake made extensive use of mines and booby traps during the Jihad, and their own mine clearance formations proved essential for maintaining supply routes through contested territory. Six-trooper Level Is provided thorough area coverage during systematic clearance operations.

Inner Sphere salvage squads organized four Groundhog operators to handle battlefield recovery operations following engagements. These squads stripped damaged BattleMechs and vehicles of usable components, recovered ammunition, and catalogued wreckage for later retrieval by heavier recovery assets. Mercenary units particularly valued the Salvage Arm configuration, as rapid post-battle recovery directly affected their operating margins.

Clan Points of Salvage Arm Groundhogs supported isorla recovery operations, cataloguing and stripping captured enemy equipment for Clan use. Five-trooper Points could process battlefield wreckage efficiently, a task typically assigned to lower-caste technicians operating under warrior caste supervision. The exoskeleton's protection allowed salvage Points to begin recovery operations while engagement areas were still being secured.

Word of Blake and ComStar Level I formations equipped with Salvage Arm Groundhogs handled equipment recovery at damaged HPG stations and military facilities. Six-trooper formations provided the manpower needed to systematically strip and recover components from battle-damaged infrastructure, a task that became increasingly common as the Jihad intensified and replacement parts grew scarce.

Inner Sphere military commands outside the Kandersteg Militia organized Hantu operators into standard four-trooper squads, integrating them into existing infantry platoon structures. Mercenary units passing through Kandersteg's hiring halls adopted the Hantu in this configuration, fielding squads as enhanced infantry elements within combined arms formations. The four-trooper squad provided a familiar organizational framework for commands already accustomed to conventional infantry doctrine.

Clan formations that acquired the Hantu organized operators into five-trooper Points following standard Clan military structure. The suit's use of stealth armor manufactured for Clan Wolf-in-Exile gave it a natural connection to Clan supply chains, though the Hantu's deliberately simplified design and lack of advanced battle armor systems limited its appeal among warrior caste personnel. Garrison and labor caste troops found the suit's accessible interface better matched to their training level.

The Hauberk saw its heaviest deployment in four-trooper squads within the Armed Forces of the Federated Suns. AFFS commanders organized their suits following standard Inner Sphere infantry doctrine, with squads operating as part of larger platoons attached to BattleMech or armored formations. The suit's defensive orientation made it well-suited to holding key positions and establishing ambush corridors while faster units maneuvered around the enemy.

Clan Diamond Shark's role in providing the Undine chassis that spawned the Hauberk led to a small number of suits finding their way back to Clan merchant networks. Those few examples organized into five-trooper Points saw limited operational use, as most Clans preferred purpose-built Clan battle armor over Inner Sphere designs.

Word of Blake forces operating on New Avalon and other Federated Suns worlds captured a number of Hauberks during the Jihad. Reorganized into six-trooper Level I formations per Com Guard doctrine, these captured suits supplemented Blakist infantry forces, though the Word's preference for its own battle armor designs limited widespread adoption.

The Commando configuration entered service primarily with AFFS four-trooper squads tasked with urban security and close-quarters operations. Its mimetic armor and reliable Inner Sphere weapons made it a preferred choice for garrison commands defending rebuilt cities and critical infrastructure in the post-Jihad Federated Suns.

The Commando's reliance on standard Inner Sphere weaponry and mimetic armor made it an unlikely candidate for Clan acquisition. Any examples organized into five-trooper Points would represent captured or salvaged suits rather than deliberate procurement, given the Clans' general preference for their own battle armor technology.

With the Commando entering production in 3088, well after the dissolution of the Word of Blake, six-trooper Level I formations would represent Republic of the Sphere or successor-state forces adopting Com Guard organizational structures. The suit's urban combat specialization made it relevant for peacekeeping and security operations.

The U15's origins as a hand-built experimental design limited its deployment to a handful of four-trooper squads on New Avalon. These suits operated under close supervision from Stevens Barracks, where Tech Sergeant Balke's small production run supplied a local battle armor unit for urban training and security operations.

The U15's heavy use of Clan-manufactured components made it theoretically compatible with Clan organizational doctrine, but the suit's experimental nature and extremely limited production run made five-trooper Point deployment effectively impossible outside of salvage scenarios.

With only a handful of U15 suits ever produced, six-trooper Level I formations of this experimental design remained purely theoretical. The suit's Clan-technology weapons and mimetic armor would have been of significant intelligence value to any Com Guard or Word of Blake unit that managed to acquire an example.

The Hauberk II saw primary deployment in AFFS four-trooper squads assigned to urban defense and close-quarters operations. Squads were typically attached to BattleMech companies or armored platoons clearing Word of Blake holdouts from Avalon City and other contested urban centers during the final years of the Jihad.

As a field-expedient refit produced exclusively for Federated Suns forces during the Jihad, the Hauberk II saw no deliberate Clan adoption. Any five-trooper Points of this design would represent captured examples organized per Clan doctrine, an unlikely scenario given the suit's limited initial production run.

Word of Blake forces battling on New Avalon would have been among the first to encounter the Hauberk II in combat, as the design was created specifically to counter Blakist battle armor in urban engagements. Captured examples reorganized into six-trooper Level I formations would have provided valuable insight into AFFS field modification capabilities.

Inner Sphere commercial operations typically organize HeavyHauler operators into four-person squads, matching standard infantry logistics doctrine. These squads rotate through loading shifts at spaceports, warehouses, and DropShip docking bays, with each operator handling a designated cargo zone. The four-trooper formation allows for efficient coordination during container transfer operations while maintaining manageable supervisory spans for civilian dock foremen.

Clan merchant and logistics castes adopted the HeavyHauler into their standard five-trooper Point organization, treating exoskeleton work crews identically to other labor formations. Points of HeavyHauler operators service Clan cargo facilities and DropShip holds, moving supplies and equipment with the same efficiency-driven discipline applied to all Clan labor operations.

ComStar and Word of Blake logistics commands organized HeavyHauler operators into six-trooper Level I formations, consistent with their broader military organizational structure. These larger work teams proved well suited to the high-volume cargo throughput demanded by HPG compound supply operations and major garrison resupply efforts, where the additional two operators per team reduced shift rotation frequency.

Inner Sphere militaries organized their Infiltrators into standard four-trooper squads following conventional infantry doctrine. AFFS and LAAF line units employed these squads for tactical reconnaissance, screening operations, and rear-area security where stealth mattered more than firepower. Integration with existing infantry command structures and BattleMech lance formations was straightforward, and the four-trooper squad became the most common fielding arrangement across both successor states.

Clan formations that captured or salvaged Infiltrator suits organized them into five-trooper Points consistent with standard Clan doctrine. Garrison and solahma formations occasionally fielded Points of captured Inner Sphere battle armor for reconnaissance duties when Elemental suits were unavailable or committed elsewhere. Clan warriors generally viewed these captured suits with disdain, though pragmatic commanders recognized their stealth value for observation missions.

ComStar and Word of Blake forces organized their Infiltrators into six-trooper Level I formations. Com Guard units deployed these formations primarily for intelligence-gathering and perimeter security around HPG compounds and other critical installations. The larger formation size provided additional sensor coverage, allowing Level I commanders to establish overlapping surveillance zones during defensive operations.

Federated Commonwealth intelligence agencies fielded the Special Ops configuration in four-trooper squads for covert operations. DMI and MIIO teams used these squads to conduct surveillance behind enemy lines, plant remote sensors along suspected supply routes, and perform targeted missions against high-value objectives. The four-trooper squad was the standard formation for these sensitive operations throughout both successor states.

403.name: Infiltrator Mk. I Battle Armor (Special Ops)(Sqd4)

text.deployment: Clan units that acquired Special Ops-configured Infiltrators organized them into five-trooper Points. Clan use of these specialized surveillance suits was rare and confined primarily to garrison forces conducting area reconnaissance where standard Clan equipment was unavailable. The enhanced sensor package offered capabilities that complemented rather than duplicated existing Clan reconnaissance assets.

404.name: Infiltrator Mk. I Battle Armor (Special Ops)(Sqd5)

text.deployment: ComStar and Word of Blake intelligence elements organized Special Ops Infiltrators into six-trooper Level I formations for dedicated surveillance and signals-monitoring operations. The additional troopers per formation provided expanded sensor dispenser coverage and allowed more effective monitoring of critical communications nodes and facilities.

405.name: Infiltrator Mk. I Battle Armor (Special Ops)(Sqd6)

text.deployment: AFFS and LAAF four-trooper squads formed the backbone of Federated Commonwealth stealth reconnaissance formations. These squads operated within Regimental Combat Teams, providing organic scouting and sniping capability. DMI and MIIO covert action teams also fielded four-trooper squads for sensitive field operations behind enemy lines, where the Puma's combination of stealth and firepower proved particularly effective.

Clan units that captured Puma suits organized them into five-trooper Points consistent with standard Clan formation doctrine. The suit offered Clan garrison commanders an infiltration tool distinct from the direct-combat-oriented Elemental. Watch and solahma formations occasionally deployed captured Puma Points for reconnaissance duties that did not warrant committing frontline Elemental assets.

ComStar and Word of Blake forces fielded the Puma in six-trooper Level I formations. Com Guard intelligence units employed these formations for perimeter surveillance and counter-infiltration operations around critical installations. Word of Blake Militia units used Level I Puma formations during the Jihad for advance reconnaissance in support of larger offensive operations.

Clan forces organized Magnetic-configured suits into five-trooper Points when captured examples became available. The magnetic clamp capability aligned well with the Clan practice of transporting battle armor on combat units, offering attachment to a wider range of vehicles and structures than standard Clan transport arrangements provided.

Word of Blake formations fielded the Magnetic configuration in six-trooper Level I formations during the Jihad. These formations attached to Blakist armored columns for mobile operations, providing dismountable reconnaissance and sniping teams that could rapidly redeploy across a fluid battlefield by clamping onto passing vehicles.

AFFS naval infantry organized Marine-configured Infiltrators into four-trooper squads for boarding actions and ship defense operations. These squads specialized in breaching operations against hostile DropShips and JumpShips, using their breaching tools to penetrate sealed compartments while engaging defenders in the tight corridors characteristic of shipboard combat.

Clan naval forces organized captured Marine variants into five-trooper Points for boarding and counter-boarding operations. The suit's stealth characteristics offered an infiltration approach to shipboard combat distinct from the direct-assault boarding tactics typically favored by Clan Elemental Points during naval engagements.

ComStar and successor organizations fielded Marine-configured Infiltrators in six-trooper Level I formations for WarShip and space station security duties. The larger formation size provided enough troopers to simultaneously breach multiple compartments during boarding actions and maintain security across broader sections of a vessel.

AFFS reconnaissance elements employed four-trooper Sensor squads for deep battlefield surveillance. These squads specialized in establishing observation posts and relaying real-time intelligence to field commanders. The enhanced detection equipment made these formations particularly valuable during defensive operations where early warning of enemy movement could determine the outcome of an engagement.

Clan formations that acquired Sensor-configured Infiltrators organized them into five-trooper Points for reconnaissance operations. The dedicated sensor package offered detection capabilities that complemented standard Clan reconnaissance assets, making these captured suits somewhat more attractive to garrison commanders than the standard Puma configuration for area surveillance duties.

ComStar and Word of Blake intelligence services organized Sensor variants into six-trooper Level I formations for dedicated area surveillance and signals monitoring. The larger formation size allowed Level I commanders to establish comprehensive sensor networks covering wider operational areas than smaller formations could manage effectively.

The Coral Intent prototypes were fielded exclusively by AFFS special operations units in four-trooper squads. Operating under Project CORAL INTENT, these experimental squads evaluated the suit's C3 targeting integration during field exercises and limited combat deployments from Achernar BattleMechs' facility on New Avalon.

417.name: Infiltrator Mk. II Battle Armor Coral Intent(Sqd4)

text.deployment: Five-trooper Coral Intent Points were assembled for evaluation in Clan-compatible organizational structures. The C3 system's force-multiplication capability was tested across a broader formation spread, though the experimental nature of the program restricted deployment to controlled evaluation scenarios and limited field trials.

418.name: Infiltrator Mk. II Battle Armor Coral Intent(Sqd5)

text.deployment: Six-trooper Coral Intent Level I formations were trialed for ComStar-compatible organizational deployment. The larger formation size permitted evaluation of networked C3 targeting across a wider distribution of troopers, testing whether the system could provide actionable data to friendly forces from multiple dispersed positions simultaneously.

419.name: Infiltrator Mk. II Battle Armor Coral Intent(Sqd6)

text.deployment: Inner Sphere military units organizing Anti-Tank Ironholds into four-trooper squads employed them as dedicated vehicle-hunting teams. These squads typically operated in pairs, using the LB-X autocannons to disable light vehicles and combat transports while the Inferno launcher targeted heavier assets. The smaller squad size allowed more flexible dispersal across a defensive sector.

Clan Jade Falcon Points fielding the Anti-Tank configuration filled a gap in Elemental tactical doctrine by providing organic anti-vehicle capability at the Point level. Five-trooper Points could concentrate autocannon fire to threaten even well-armored combat vehicles, while the Inferno launchers added a heat-based disruption element. These Points typically operated in conjunction with standard Ironhold Points, creating combined-arms Elemental formations capable of engaging both infantry and vehicle targets.

Level I formations of six Anti-Tank Ironholds provided formidable anti-vehicle screens for ComStar and Word of Blake defensive positions. The concentrated LB-X autocannon fire from six suits could threaten medium-weight combat vehicles, while the Inferno SRM launchers created hazardous chokepoints for advancing armor columns. These larger formations compensated for the one-shot nature of the SRM launcher by ensuring multiple launchers were available per engagement.

Inner Sphere forces fielding the Fire Ironhold in four-trooper squads leveraged the configuration's quadruple Gauss armament to create dense anti-infantry kill zones. Without jump capability, these squads relied on vehicular transport or BattleMech attachment to reach combat positions. The fire-resistant armor provided useful protection when operating alongside incendiary-equipped allied forces in urban clearance operations.

Jade Falcon Points equipped with the Fire variant operated as dedicated assault elements, typically deployed against fortified positions where the quadruple Anti-Personnel Gauss Rifle loadout could suppress defending infantry. The lack of jump jets forced these Points into more linear assault approaches, often riding OmniMechs directly into enemy defensive perimeters before dismounting at close range. Falcon commanders valued the Fire configuration for breaking entrenched defenders.

ComStar and Word of Blake Level I formations using the Fire Ironhold concentrated six suits' worth of anti-personnel Gauss fire into overwhelming barrages. These formations excelled in defensive operations, where the lack of jump mobility mattered less than raw sustained firepower. The fire-resistant armor offered additional protection against the incendiary weapons commonly employed by Blakist forces during the Jihad.

Inner Sphere military formations that acquired Ironhold suits through salvage or Trials of Possession organized them into four-trooper squads consistent with standard infantry doctrine. These smaller units typically operated alongside conventional infantry platoons, providing anti-personnel firepower that organic forces could not match. The jump-capable standard model proved well-suited to squad-level tactics emphasizing building-to-building movement in urban operations.

Clan Jade Falcon Elemental Points of five troopers formed the primary operational unit for the standard Ironhold. Points deployed from OmniMech transports to seize key terrain, exploit breaches in enemy lines, and conduct anti-infantry sweeps. The jump-capable configuration allowed Falcon Points to operate across broken terrain where heavier assault armor would be confined to ground-level approaches. The Third Falcon Talon Cluster fielded entire Stars of Ironhold Points during the late Jihad.

ComStar and Word of Blake Level I formations of six troopers represented the largest standard Ironhold tactical groupings. These oversized units concentrated the suit's Gauss firepower into devastating volleys, though the additional troopers placed greater strain on transport logistics. Level I Ironhold elements typically supported larger Com Guard or Militia Level II formations during the Jihad, providing dedicated anti-infantry screening.

The Hive configuration was fielded exclusively by the "Four Myths and a Funeral" Gladiator team on Galatea, operating as a four-trooper squad in the arena circuit. The C3 networking between the Hive suits and the team's modified Manticore gave them a decisive coordination advantage in arena combat, directing concentrated fire with precision unusual for battle armor formations.

Five-trooper Points equipped with the Hive configuration existed primarily as a theoretical organizational option. The custom arena refit's experimental C3 system and specialized nature limited its adoption beyond the original Galatean Gladiator team, though the Point formation offered additional networked targeting nodes for the C3 system.

Six-trooper Level I formations mounting the Hive configuration represented an organizational variant for commands following ComStar doctrine. The experimental nature of the battle armor C3 system and the refit's arena-specific origins made large-scale adoption impractical, though the expanded network of six targeting nodes maximized the C3 system's coordination potential.

Inner Sphere commanders deployed flamer-equipped squads of four troopers primarily for urban clearance and anti-infantry patrol operations. The four-trooper squad structure matched standard infantry doctrine, allowing direct attachment to BattleMech lances on a one-to-one basis. Flamer squads were particularly common in garrison and counterinsurgency roles across all Great House militaries.

Five-trooper Points of flamer-equipped IS Standard suits were fielded by formations following Clan-pattern organization. Wolf's Dragoons and other units with Clan heritage organized captured or purchased Inner Sphere equipment into traditional Point structures, valuing the additional trooper for the increased area denial provided by massed flamer fire.

ComStar's Com Guard and the Word of Blake Militia organized flamer-equipped IS Standard suits into six-trooper Level I formations. The larger formation size provided additional suppressive firepower in building clearance and perimeter defense operations. Com Guard units particularly favored the flamer loadout for defensive engagements around HPG compound facilities.

Small laser-equipped squads of four were among the most widely deployed IS Standard configurations across the Great Houses. The energy weapon's independence from ammunition supply chains made it popular with commands operating on extended deployments. Infantry platoons built around laser squads maintained combat effectiveness longer in the field than those dependent on ballistic resupply.

Five-trooper Points carrying small lasers operated within Clan-influenced formations, where the energy weapon's logistical simplicity proved attractive for commands maintaining mixed Inner Sphere and Clan equipment. The laser loadout reduced the supply burden on formations already managing multiple ammunition types across diverse equipment inventories.

Com Guard Level I formations equipped with small lasers were deployed as general-purpose battle armor elements within combined-arms Level II and Level III commands. The Word of Blake Militia maintained similar organization, favoring the laser configuration for its endurance during extended garrison and occupation operations throughout the Jihad.

Light recoilless rifle-equipped squads first saw widespread deployment during the Capellan-St. Ives War in 3061. Four-trooper squads carried the LRR as a compromise between the machine gun's anti-infantry lethality and the SRM's anti-armor punch. The configuration became popular across multiple Great House armies as a general-purpose combat loadout.

Five-trooper Points armed with light recoilless rifles served in formations adopting Clan organizational patterns. The LRR's balanced capability profile made it well-suited for Points operating independently or in screening roles ahead of heavier formations, where engagement targets could range from infantry to light vehicles without warning.

Com Guard and Word of Blake forces fielded LRR-equipped Level I formations as general-purpose battle armor elements capable of engaging both infantry and light armored threats. The six-trooper formation's combined recoilless rifle fire provided effective suppression against fortified positions and light vehicle formations during offensive operations.

Inner Sphere four-trooper squads equipped with the Magnetic variant exploited the magnetic clamp system to ride into battle on friendly BattleMechs and combat vehicles, solving the chronic transport shortage that hampered conventional battle armor formations. Squad-level commanders valued the improved jump range for rapid repositioning during fluid engagements.

Five-trooper Points fielding the Magnetic modernization operated within Clan-pattern formations, where the magnetic clamp's ability to attach to any vehicle eliminated dependence on OmniMech handholds. Points could mount conventional vehicles and BattleMechs alike, restoring the mechanized mobility that Inner Sphere battle armor often lacked.

Six-trooper Level I formations with the Magnetic variant served in commands following ComStar organizational doctrine. The magnetic clamp system allowed the larger formation to distribute across multiple transport vehicles, maintaining tactical cohesion while keeping pace with mechanized advances without dedicated OmniMech transport assets.

Machine gun-equipped squads served as dedicated anti-infantry screening elements within Great House commands. Four-trooper squads were attached to frontline BattleMech lances to suppress enemy conventional infantry attempting to close on friendly assets. The machine gun's lethality against unarmored targets made these squads effective deterrents during combined-arms operations.

Five-trooper Points armed with machine guns operated in formations that adopted Clan organizational conventions. The additional trooper per formation increased the volume of suppressive fire, making machine gun Points effective in both offensive sweeps and defensive perimeter security across varied terrain.

Com Guard and Word of Blake forces organized machine gun-equipped suits into six-trooper Level I formations for base defense and security patrol duties. The higher trooper count per formation provided sustained automatic fire coverage across wider defensive frontages, complementing the larger formation's ability to hold ground without BattleMech support.

SRM-equipped squads of four troopers were reserved for anti-BattleMech operations where their single-use missiles could be employed at decisive moments. Standard infantry doctrine paired SRM squads with laser or machine gun squads, allowing the missile-armed troopers to concentrate fire against armored targets while their companions provided covering fire against infantry threats.

Five-trooper Points carrying one-shot SRM launchers operated within Clan-pattern formations, where the additional missile trooper increased the probability of achieving a mission kill against an armored target. The concentrated volley from five SRM-2 launchers posed a credible threat even to assault-weight BattleMechs at close range.

Com Guard and Militia Level I formations armed with SRM launchers were employed as dedicated anti-armor reaction elements. The six-trooper formation concentrated enough missile firepower to threaten heavy vehicles and BattleMechs in a single coordinated volley. These units were held in reserve and committed against priority armored targets during defensive engagements.
